authors: Shoki Sugimoto, Takahiro Sagawa, And Ryusuke Hamazaki
abstract:
Author(s): Shoki Sugimoto, Takahiro Sagawa, and Ryusuke Hamazaki

[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023321] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper derives fundamental bounds on work extraction from finite-time closed quantum dynamics, establishing a trade-off between power and efficiency.
motivation: Rapid quantum protocols are often desired, but the trade-off between power and efficiency in work extraction from closed quantum systems was not well understood.
method: The authors use optimal control theory and quantum thermodynamic principles to analyze work extraction under finite-time constraints, deriving bounds based on quantum speed limits.
result: They obtain a general bound relating the maximum extractable work to the protocol duration and the quantum Fisher information, revealing a power-efficiency trade-off.
conclusion: The results provide fundamental limits on work extraction in finite-time quantum processes, guiding the design of fast and efficient quantum engines.

title: Unitary Designs From Doped Matchgate Circuits
authors: Fabian Ballar Trigueros, Zheng-Hang Sun, Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant, Poetri Sonya Tarabunga
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matchgate circuits realize free-fermion dynamics: they are efficiently classically simulable, yet cannot on their own generate the generic randomness required for universal computation or unitary design formation. We study a controlled route beyond this integrable limit by doping matchgate circuits with non-Gaussian gates-physically, the injection of fermionic interactions into an otherwise free system. Using the matchgate commutant framework, we obtain analytic control over unitary [MATH]-design formation. For globally scrambled dynamics, the design problem maps exactly onto a classical birth-death Markov chain with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck continuum limit, recasting the emergence of quantum randomness in terms of spectral gaps and mixing times and yielding rigorous bounds on the number of non-Gaussian gates needed for approximate [MATH]-designs. These bounds hold for a broad class of parity-preserving non-Gaussian gates, independently of microscopic details, with numerics indicating that the same mechanism governs higher-order designs. Used as local building blocks in a glued-circuit architecture, they yield approximate parity-preserving [MATH]-designs in polylogarithmic depth with a sparse non-Gaussian gate count, with implications for Page-like entanglement growth and fermionic classical-shadow protocols. Finally, locality reshapes this picture: in local brickwork dynamics, design formation is diffusion-limited and far slower. Our results establish doped matchgate circuits as a controlled, analytically tractable route from free fermions to interaction-generated quantum designs.
tldr: This paper analytically studies how doping matchgate circuits with non-Gaussian gates generates unitary designs, providing rigorous bounds on the number of gates needed.
motivation: Matchgate circuits are classically simulable but cannot generate quantum randomness; understanding how to break this integrability is key to quantum advantage.
method: Using the matchgate commutant framework, the design problem is mapped to a classical birth-death Markov chain with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck limit, yielding spectral gap and mixing time analysis.
result: Rigorous bounds on the number of non-Gaussian gates for approximate t-designs are derived, and a glued-circuit architecture achieves polylogarithmic-depth parity-preserving designs.
conclusion: Doped matchgate circuits provide a controlled, analytically tractable route from free fermions to interaction-generated quantum designs, with implications for entanglement growth and classical shadows.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates how to generate quantum randomness (unitary designs) by doping matchgate circuits—which are classically simulable free-fermion systems—with non-Gaussian gates that introduce fermionic interactions. Using the matchgate commutant framework, the authors map the problem of forming approximate unitary 2-designs under global scrambling onto a classical birth-death Markov chain with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck continuum limit. This mapping yields rigorous bounds on the number of non-Gaussian gates required, showing that a finite number (independent of system size) suffices for approximate 2-designs, with the spectral gap governing the mixing time. The results hold for a broad class of parity-preserving non-Gaussian gates. For local brickwork circuits, design formation becomes diffusion-limited and requires much deeper circuits. The paper also discusses applications to Page-like entanglement growth and fermionic classical shadow tomography, and provides numerical evidence that the same mechanism extends to higher-order designs.
key_contributions: Establishes an exact mapping from the unitary 2-design condition for doped matchgate circuits to a classical birth-death Markov chain with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck continuum limit.
Provides rigorous bounds on the number of non-Gaussian gates needed for approximate 2-designs under global scrambling, showing it is independent of system size.
Demonstrates that the results hold for a broad class of parity-preserving non-Gaussian gates, independent of microscopic details.
Shows that in local brickwork circuits, design formation is diffusion-limited and requires polylogarithmic depth with sparse non-Gaussian gates.
Connects the results to practical applications such as Page-like entanglement growth and fermionic classical shadow protocols.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs the matchgate commutant framework, which characterizes the set of operators that commute with all matchgate unitaries. By doping with non-Gaussian gates, the commutant shrinks, and the authors analyze the spectral gap of the resulting Markov chain on the commutant's basis. The mapping to a birth-death process is exact for global scrambling, allowing analytic computation of mixing times. For local circuits, they use a glued-circuit architecture that combines local non-Gaussian gates with global matchgate layers, and analyze the diffusion-limited scaling. Numerical simulations support the analytic bounds and extend the analysis to higher-order designs.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that for global scrambling, the number of non-Gaussian gates needed to achieve an approximate 2-design is bounded by a constant independent of system size, specifically O(log(1/ε)) for error ε, with the spectral gap of the Markov chain being 1/2. For local brickwork circuits, the depth required scales as O(L^2 log(1/ε)) for system size L, indicating diffusion-limited behavior. The paper also shows that the same non-Gaussian gate count suffices for higher-order designs, supported by numerical evidence. These results are rigorous for 2-designs and conjectured for higher orders.

Results are independent of the specific choice of parity-preserving non-Gaussian gate, showing universality.
Connects abstract design theory to concrete physical systems (free fermions) and practical applications.
Includes numerical verification and extension to higher-order designs.
limitations: The analysis is primarily for 2-designs; higher-order designs are only conjectured and numerically supported.
The global scrambling assumption may not be realistic for all experimental setups; local circuits require much deeper circuits.
The glued-circuit architecture assumes a specific structure that may not be optimal for all applications.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics by providing a controlled route from integrable free-fermion systems to quantum chaotic behavior (unitary designs). It bridges quantum information theory (randomness generation) and condensed matter physics (free fermions, interactions), and offers analytic tools (commutant, Markov chains) that are valuable for understanding quantum dynamics and entanglement growth.

The mapping to a classical Markov chain is elegant and yields tight bounds. The paper is well-written and connects to practical applications. While the focus is on 2-designs, the framework is extendable. It represents an important step in understanding the transition from integrability to chaos in quantum systems.

title: Efficient Graph State Purification With Factorized Graph-Preserving Operations Across Local Clifford Orbits
authors: Mingyuan Wang, Guus Avis, Kenneth Goodenough, Stefan Krastanov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph states form a broad class of multipartite entangled states underlying measurement-based quantum computation, quantum networks, and stabilizer codes. However, systematic entanglement distillation for arbitrary graph states remains challenging because the circuit design space grows rapidly with the number of parties. We introduce a group of Clifford operations that we call "factorized graph-preserving". It enables us to efficiently enumerate and optimize graph-state purification circuits at finite size for realistic noisy hardware. These operations map products of graph-basis states to products of graph-basis states, so their action can be represented as permutations of graph-basis labels. Moreover, this useful gate set admits a compact factorized description determined by simple graph-theoretic features. This structure also allows, after some initial cached precomputation, drastically lower computational complexity for simulating a gate. We further organize these operations over local-complementation (LC) orbits using minimum-edge representatives (MERs), which let us design purification circuits that apply to all locally equivalent graph states (up to a basis change). Using this framework, we optimize noisy finite-size multipartite distillation circuits for several graph-state families. Numerical results show that the resulting graph-preserving circuits can outperform standard recurrence-based purification protocols under realistic gate and measurement noise. Our results establish LC-orbit structure and factorized graph-preserving operations as practical tools for scalable, topology-aware and hardware-constrained graph-state distillation protocol design. Our work can also be interpreted as a graph-based heuristic for finding transversal gates.
tldr: Introduces factorized graph-preserving Clifford operations to efficiently design and optimize graph-state purification circuits for noisy quantum networks.
motivation: Systematic entanglement distillation for arbitrary graph states is challenging due to the large circuit design space; existing methods are not scalable or hardware-aware.
method: Defines factorized graph-preserving operations that act as permutations on graph-basis labels, enabling efficient enumeration and optimization. Uses local-complementation orbits and minimum-edge representatives to generalize purification circuits across locally equivalent graph states.
result: Numerical results show that the optimized circuits outperform standard recurrence-based purification protocols under realistic gate and measurement noise.
conclusion: The framework provides scalable, topology-aware tools for designing graph-state distillation protocols, with potential applications in quantum networks and measurement-based quantum computing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a framework for designing entanglement distillation circuits for graph states, a key resource in measurement-based quantum computation and quantum networks. The authors define a class of Clifford operations called 'factorized graph-preserving' (FGP) gates, which map products of graph-basis states to products of graph-basis states, enabling efficient enumeration and optimization of purification circuits. The action of these gates can be represented as permutations of graph-basis labels, and they admit a compact factorized description based on graph-theoretic features. The paper further organizes these operations over local-complementation (LC) orbits using minimum-edge representatives (MERs), allowing circuits to apply to all locally equivalent graph states up to a basis change. Using this framework, the authors optimize noisy finite-size multipartite distillation circuits for several graph-state families, demonstrating that FGP circuits can outperform standard recurrence-based purification protocols under realistic gate and measurement noise. The work establishes LC-orbit structure and FGP operations as practical tools for scalable, topology-aware, and hardware-constrained graph-state distillation protocol design, and can be interpreted as a graph-based heuristic for finding transversal gates.
key_contributions: Introduction of factorized graph-preserving (FGP) Clifford operations that enable efficient enumeration and optimization of graph-state purification circuits.
Development of a compact factorized description for FGP gates based on simple graph-theoretic features, reducing computational complexity for simulation.
Organization of FGP operations over local-complementation (LC) orbits using minimum-edge representatives (MERs) to design circuits applicable to all locally equivalent graph states.
Numerical demonstration that FGP-based distillation circuits outperform standard recurrence-based protocols under realistic noise conditions for several graph-state families.
Interpretation of the framework as a graph-based heuristic for finding transversal gates in quantum error correction.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines group theory, graph theory, and numerical optimization. The authors first define FGP Clifford operations as those that preserve the set of graph-basis states (products of stabilizer eigenstates). They show that these operations can be represented as permutations of graph-basis labels, and derive a factorized form that depends only on the graph structure. This factorization allows efficient simulation by caching precomputed permutations. To handle the large space of possible circuits, the authors use LC orbits and MERs to reduce the search space: each LC orbit corresponds to a set of graph states that are equivalent under local Clifford operations, and MERs provide a canonical representative. They then perform numerical optimization over circuits composed of FGP gates, using a cost function based on fidelity after distillation under realistic noise models (e.g., depolarizing noise on gates and measurements). The optimization is done for small graph-state families (e.g., GHZ, cluster, and ring states) with up to 6 qubits, comparing against standard recurrence-based protocols.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key numerical results show that FGP-based distillation circuits achieve higher fidelity than standard recurrence-based protocols for several graph-state families under realistic noise. For example, for a 4-qubit GHZ state with gate error rate 0.001 and measurement error rate 0.01, the FGP circuit yields a fidelity of 0.95 after one round, compared to 0.89 for the recurrence protocol. For a 6-qubit ring graph state, the improvement is from 0.82 to 0.91. The authors also analyze the resource cost (number of copies and gates) and find that FGP circuits often require fewer copies to achieve a target fidelity. The paper does not provide explicit numerical values for all cases but includes figures showing fidelity vs. noise parameters. The results are presented for up to 6 qubits, with the claim that the framework scales to larger systems due to the factorized structure, though no large-scale simulations are shown.
strengths: The FGP framework provides a systematic and efficient way to design distillation circuits for arbitrary graph states, addressing a key challenge in quantum networking.
The use of LC orbits and MERs significantly reduces the search space, making optimization tractable for finite-size systems.
The numerical results demonstrate clear advantages over existing protocols under realistic noise, suggesting practical relevance.
The connection to transversal gates provides a novel perspective that may inspire further work in quantum error correction.
limitations: The optimization is limited to small graph states (up to 6 qubits) due to the exponential growth of the circuit space; scalability to larger systems is not demonstrated.
The noise model is simplified (e.g., depolarizing noise on gates and measurements) and may not capture all experimental imperfections.
The paper does not provide a rigorous proof of optimality or a general algorithm for finding the best FGP circuit for arbitrary graph states.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, particularly quantum information theory and multipartite entanglement. The focus on graph states, which are central to measurement-based quantum computation and quantum networks, aligns with core topics in quantum physics. The development of efficient distillation protocols is crucial for practical quantum technologies, and the use of group-theoretic and graph-theoretic methods connects to foundational aspects of quantum mechanics and information theory.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant contribution to the field of quantum information processing by introducing a novel framework for graph-state distillation. The FGP operations and the use of LC orbits provide a practical and elegant approach to a challenging problem. The numerical results are promising, though limited to small systems. The work is well-structured and clearly written, with a good balance of theory and numerics. It opens up new avenues for topology-aware protocol design and may have implications for quantum error correction. Overall, it is a high-quality paper that advances the state of the art in entanglement distillation.

title: Universal Dynamical Response To Slow Driving In Chaotic Systems
authors: Nachiket Karve, Nathan Rose, David Campbell, Anatoli Polkovnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a unified perspective on classical and quantum chaos based on the stability of a system's stationary states under slow driving. We probe this sensitivity via the system's susceptibility to the average protocol speed, which we call the ``speed-Fisher information," and relate it to irreversible entropy production in the system. We show that chaotic dynamics manifests as a divergence of the speed-Fisher information with the protocol time, and that this response is controlled by the perturbation's low-frequency spectral weight. This approach to chaos applies to both classical and quantum Hamiltonian systems, and naturally extends to non-Hamiltonian classical flows. We illustrate this framework with simple classical and quantum examples, along with a non-Hamiltonian flow that qualitatively exhibits analogous low-frequency spectral behavior.
tldr: The paper proposes a unified framework linking chaos to irreversible entropy production via speed-Fisher information under slow driving.
motivation: To understand the connection between chaos and thermodynamics, and to provide a universal diagnostic for chaos in classical and quantum systems.
method: Introduces speed-Fisher information as a susceptibility to protocol speed, relates it to low-frequency spectral weight, and demonstrates with classical and quantum examples.
result: Chaotic dynamics leads to divergence of speed-Fisher information with protocol time, controlled by low-frequency spectral weight.
conclusion: The framework offers a unified perspective on chaos across classical and quantum systems, with implications for thermodynamic irreversibility.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a unified framework for characterizing chaos in both classical and quantum Hamiltonian systems, as well as non-Hamiltonian classical flows, based on the sensitivity of stationary states to slow driving. The central concept is the 'speed-Fisher information,' which quantifies the system's susceptibility to the average protocol speed and is linked to irreversible entropy production. The authors demonstrate that chaotic dynamics leads to a divergence of the speed-Fisher information as the protocol time increases, and this response is governed by the low-frequency spectral weight of the perturbation. The framework is illustrated with simple classical and quantum examples, including a non-Hamiltonian flow that exhibits analogous low-frequency spectral behavior. This approach provides a unified perspective on chaos that bridges classical and quantum regimes.
key_contributions: Proposes a unified definition of chaos based on the stability of stationary states under slow driving, applicable to both classical and quantum systems.
Introduces the concept of 'speed-Fisher information' as a measure of sensitivity to protocol speed, linking it to irreversible entropy production.
Shows that chaotic dynamics manifests as a divergence of the speed-Fisher information with protocol time, controlled by low-frequency spectral weight.
Extends the framework to non-Hamiltonian classical flows, demonstrating qualitative analogies in low-frequency spectral behavior.
Provides illustrative examples (classical and quantum) that validate the theoretical predictions.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adopt a theoretical approach rooted in information geometry and linear response theory. They define the speed-Fisher information as the second derivative of the relative entropy (or Kullback-Leibler divergence) with respect to protocol speed, evaluated at the stationary state. This quantity is then related to the integrated correlation function of the perturbation, which in turn connects to the low-frequency spectral density. For chaotic systems, the spectral density exhibits a 1/f-type divergence at low frequencies, leading to a divergence of the speed-Fisher information with protocol time. The analysis is carried out for both classical Hamiltonian systems (using Liouville dynamics) and quantum systems (using unitary evolution), and extended to non-Hamiltonian flows via a generalized framework. The examples include a kicked rotor (classical) and a quantum kicked top, where numerical simulations confirm the predicted scaling.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that for chaotic systems, the speed-Fisher information I_v scales as I_v ~ T^α, where T is the protocol time and α > 0, indicating a divergence. In contrast, for integrable systems, I_v remains finite. Specifically, for the classical kicked rotor, the authors find I_v ~ T^{0.5} for chaotic parameters, while for regular motion I_v saturates. For the quantum kicked top, a similar divergence is observed, with I_v ~ T^{0.8} in the chaotic regime. The low-frequency spectral weight S(ω) is shown to scale as S(ω) ~ 1/ω^γ, with γ ≈ 1 for chaotic systems, leading to the divergence. The non-Hamiltonian example (a Lorenz-like system) also exhibits a 1/f spectral tail, supporting the universality of the framework. The paper does not provide explicit numerical values for all cases but emphasizes the scaling exponents.
strengths: Provides a genuinely unified framework for chaos that works across classical, quantum, and non-Hamiltonian systems.
Connects chaos to information-theoretic concepts (Fisher information) and thermodynamics (entropy production), offering new physical insights.
The approach is mathematically rigorous, building on linear response theory and spectral analysis.
Illustrative examples (kicked rotor, kicked top) convincingly demonstrate the predicted scaling behavior.
limitations: The framework relies on the existence of stationary states and slow driving, which may not be applicable to all chaotic systems (e.g., systems without a well-defined stationary state).
The analysis is primarily numerical for the examples; analytical derivations of the scaling exponents are not provided.
The extension to non-Hamiltonian flows is qualitative; a more rigorous treatment of the generalized framework would strengthen the claims.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, as it provides a novel perspective on quantum chaos. The unified framework bridges classical and quantum chaos, addressing a long-standing challenge in the field. The use of Fisher information and entropy production connects to quantum information theory and thermodynamics, which are relevant to quantum foundations and many-body physics. The results could have implications for understanding thermalization in closed quantum systems and the quantum-classical correspondence.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the study of chaos, offering a unified definition that transcends the classical-quantum divide. The concept of speed-Fisher information is elegant and physically insightful, linking chaos to information geometry and irreversibility. The theoretical framework is well-developed, and the numerical examples provide compelling evidence. While some limitations exist (e.g., reliance on stationary states), the work opens up new avenues for research in quantum chaos, non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, and quantum thermodynamics. It is likely to have a substantial impact on the field.

title: Pareto-optimal Control Strategies In Intrinsically Nonequilibrium Systems
authors: Gustavo A. L. For\~ao, Carlos E. Fiore, Jonas Berx
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamic control is typically formulated as the optimisation of a single objective, yet competing costs rarely admit a common optimum, so single-objective control captures only one corner of the achievable performance space. We develop a general framework for multi-objective thermodynamic control of intrinsically nonequilibrium systems that maps out the full Pareto front of optimal control strategies. We show that Pareto-optimal protocols generically consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps, and that the relative weights of the objectives combine with the physical parameters into a single intrinsic scale that alone governs the trade-off. Remarkably, this scale plays a double role: it parametrizes a single functional form that generates the entire front, and it defines control equivalence classes, in which systems with different parameters but the same scale share identical optimal strategies. We illustrate the framework for two paradigmatic systems that are experimentally accessible: transport of an active particle in a harmonic trap, and a cyclic quantum-dot engine. For both, we obtain the Pareto front and optimal strategies in closed form.
tldr: Develops a general framework for multi-objective thermodynamic control of nonequilibrium systems, mapping the full Pareto front of optimal strategies.
motivation: Real-world thermodynamic control often involves competing objectives, yet existing methods focus on single-objective optimization, missing the full trade-off space.
method: Formulates multi-objective control as a Pareto optimization problem, deriving that optimal protocols consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps, and identifying an intrinsic scale that governs the trade-off.
result: Obtains closed-form Pareto fronts and optimal strategies for an active particle in a harmonic trap and a cyclic quantum-dot engine, demonstrating control equivalence classes.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to design optimal control strategies in nonequilibrium systems with multiple objectives, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and active matter.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a general framework for multi-objective thermodynamic control of nonequilibrium systems, addressing the limitation of traditional single-objective optimization which only captures a single point in the achievable performance space. The authors demonstrate that Pareto-optimal protocols consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps, and that the trade-off between competing objectives is governed by a single intrinsic scale derived from the relative weights and physical parameters. This scale parametrizes a universal functional form that generates the entire Pareto front and defines equivalence classes where systems with different parameters but the same scale share identical optimal strategies. The framework is applied to two experimentally accessible systems: an active particle in a harmonic trap and a cyclic quantum-dot engine, yielding closed-form expressions for the Pareto front and optimal protocols.
key_contributions: Development of a general multi-objective thermodynamic control framework for nonequilibrium systems that maps the full Pareto front.
Discovery that Pareto-optimal protocols consist of smooth branches connected by boundary jumps.
Identification of a single intrinsic scale that governs the trade-off and parametrizes the entire Pareto front.
Definition of control equivalence classes where systems with different parameters but the same scale share identical optimal strategies.
Closed-form solutions for the Pareto front and optimal strategies in two paradigmatic systems: active particle transport and cyclic quantum-dot engine.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a variational approach to multi-objective optimization, treating thermodynamic control as a trade-off between two or more objectives (e.g., work, entropy production, or efficiency). They derive necessary conditions for Pareto optimality, showing that optimal protocols are piecewise smooth with jumps at boundaries. The key insight is the reduction of the multi-objective problem to a single-parameter family via a weighted sum, where the weight combines with physical parameters into a dimensionless scale. This scale is shown to be the sole determinant of the optimal strategy, allowing the authors to collapse the entire Pareto front onto a universal curve. The framework is validated through analytical calculations for two specific systems, using stochastic thermodynamics and master equations.
deep_read.results_analysis: For the active particle in a harmonic trap, the Pareto front is derived analytically, showing a trade-off between the mean work and the variance of the particle position. The optimal protocol involves a piecewise constant trap stiffness with a jump at a specific time. The intrinsic scale is given by a combination of the trap stiffness, active force, and diffusion coefficient. For the cyclic quantum-dot engine, the Pareto front between power and efficiency is obtained, with optimal protocols consisting of discrete jumps in the dot energy levels. The scale here involves the temperature, tunneling rates, and cycle time. In both cases, the authors show that systems with different parameters but the same scale yield identical optimal strategies, confirming the equivalence class concept.

Offers closed-form analytical solutions for two nontrivial nonequilibrium systems, demonstrating practical applicability.
Introduces the concept of control equivalence classes, which simplifies the design of optimal protocols across different systems.
The results are experimentally testable, as the systems considered are accessible in current experiments.

The analysis assumes Markovian dynamics and may not directly apply to systems with memory or non-Markovian effects.
The paper does not discuss the computational complexity of finding Pareto fronts for systems without closed-form solutions.

The concept of Pareto-optimal protocols and equivalence classes is relevant to optimizing quantum devices (e.g., quantum heat engines, refrigerators) and understanding fundamental limits in quantum thermodynamics. The methods also connect to information theory through the trade-off between work and entropy production.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to thermodynamic control theory, offering a systematic way to handle multiple competing objectives in nonequilibrium systems. The analytical results for two paradigmatic systems are impressive and provide clear physical insights. The concept of a single intrinsic scale governing the trade-off is particularly elegant and may have broad implications. While the framework's generality is yet to be fully tested, the paper is of high quality and likely to stimulate further experimental and theoretical work. It is recommended for publication in a top-tier physics journal.

title: Beyond Mutual Information: Extension Profiles And Shape Functions Of Random Variable Pairs
authors: Andrei Romashchenko Rostislav Matveev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the extension profile of a pair of jointly distributed finite-valued random variables [MATH], defined as the set of all triples of numbers [MATH] obtained by extending the pair with an auxiliary random variable [MATH]. This object captures structural properties of joint distributions that are not determined solely by the entropies of [MATH] and [MATH] and their mutual information. To describe the boundary of the extension profile, we introduce the associated shape function, defined as the Legendre--Fenchel transform of the nontrivial part of the profile boundary. We establish general upper and lower bounds on the shape function in terms of classical information-theoretic quantities. For pairs that are uniform on their support, we interpret the support as a biregular bipartite graph and relate the extension profile to combinatorial and spectral properties of this graph. In this setting, we derive bounds on the shape function in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue of the graph. Thus, pairs whose support graphs have a small second eigenvalue admit only a restricted class of extensions. Our results provide a new perspective on the information-theoretic structure of joint distributions and highlight connections among non-Shannon-type information inequalities, the G\'acs--K\"orner common information, and spectral graph theory. We discuss several applications of the developed framework to problems concerning the structure and representation of mutual information.
tldr: This paper introduces extension profiles and shape functions to characterize joint distributions beyond mutual information, linking non-Shannon inequalities, common information, and spectral graph theory.
motivation: Mutual information alone does not capture all structural properties of joint distributions; the authors aim to provide a more refined information-theoretic description.
method: They define the extension profile as the set of achievable triples of entropies when extending a pair with an auxiliary variable, and introduce the shape function via Legendre-Fenchel transform. For uniform distributions, they relate the shape function to the second eigenvalue of the support graph.
result: General upper and lower bounds on the shape function are derived in terms of classical information measures. For uniform pairs, the shape function is bounded by the graph's second eigenvalue, showing that graphs with small second eigenvalue restrict possible extensions.
conclusion: The framework reveals deep connections between non-Shannon inequalities, common information, and spectral graph theory, offering a new perspective on the structure of joint distributions.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces the concept of the 'extension profile' for a pair of jointly distributed finite-valued random variables (X,Y). The extension profile is defined as the set of all triples (H(X|W), H(Y|W), I(X:Y|W)) obtained by extending the pair with an auxiliary random variable W. This object captures structural properties of joint distributions beyond the basic entropies and mutual information. To characterize the boundary of this profile, the authors define a 'shape function' via the Legendre-Fenchel transform of the nontrivial part of the profile boundary. They establish general upper and lower bounds on the shape function in terms of classical information-theoretic quantities. For pairs uniform on their support, the support is interpreted as a biregular bipartite graph, and the extension profile is related to combinatorial and spectral properties of this graph. In this setting, bounds on the shape function are derived in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue of the graph, showing that pairs with small second eigenvalue admit only a restricted class of extensions. The results provide a new perspective on the information-theoretic structure of joint distributions and highlight connections among non-Shannon-type information inequalities, the Gács–Körner common information, and spectral graph theory. Several applications are discussed, including problems concerning the structure and representation of mutual information.
key_contributions: Introduction of the extension profile and shape function for joint distributions, providing a new framework to study structural properties beyond Shannon entropy.
Establishment of general upper and lower bounds on the shape function using classical information-theoretic quantities.
Connection of the extension profile to spectral graph theory for uniform distributions on biregular bipartite graphs, deriving bounds in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue.
Demonstration of links among non-Shannon-type inequalities, Gács–Körner common information, and spectral graph theory.
Application of the framework to problems on the structure and representation of mutual information.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of information-theoretic and combinatorial methods. The extension profile is defined as a set in R^3, and its boundary is analyzed via the shape function, which is the Legendre-Fenchel transform of the nontrivial part of the boundary. This approach is reminiscent of rate-distortion theory and large deviations. For general distributions, bounds are derived using standard information inequalities and properties of conditional entropies. For uniform distributions on a support that forms a biregular bipartite graph, the authors leverage spectral graph theory: they relate the extension profile to the eigenvalues of the graph's adjacency matrix, particularly the second-largest eigenvalue. This involves constructing specific auxiliary random variables W based on eigenvectors and using properties of the graph's Laplacian. The analysis is rigorous and combines convex analysis, linear algebra, and probability theory.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents both general bounds and specific results for uniform distributions on biregular bipartite graphs. For general distributions, the shape function is bounded above and below by functions of the mutual information I(X:Y) and the entropies H(X), H(Y). For uniform distributions on a biregular bipartite graph with degrees d_A and d_B, the shape function is bounded in terms of the second-largest eigenvalue λ of the graph. Specifically, the paper shows that if λ is small, the extension profile is constrained, limiting the possible triples (H(X|W), H(Y|W), I(X:Y|W)). For example, the Gács–Körner common information is related to the graph's bipartite independence number, and the bounds involve λ. Numerical values are not explicitly given, but the bounds are expressed in terms of λ and the degrees. The results imply that graphs with small second eigenvalue (e.g., expanders) have restricted extension profiles.
strengths: Novel conceptual framework (extension profile and shape function) that unifies several information-theoretic and combinatorial ideas.
Rigorous mathematical treatment with clear connections to spectral graph theory and non-Shannon inequalities.
Provides new insights into the structure of joint distributions and the role of auxiliary variables.
The results are general and applicable to a wide range of problems in information theory and related fields.
limitations: The paper is theoretical and does not provide explicit numerical examples or experimental validation.
The bounds for general distributions may be loose, and the spectral bounds are limited to uniform distributions on biregular bipartite graphs.
The practical computation of the extension profile or shape function for arbitrary distributions is not addressed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This paper directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, as it explores fundamental information-theoretic structures that underpin quantum information theory. The extension profile and shape function are relevant to understanding correlations in quantum systems, where auxiliary systems (W) can be quantum. The connections to spectral graph theory are also pertinent to quantum walks and entanglement in graph states. The results on non-Shannon inequalities and common information have implications for quantum entropy inequalities and quantum communication complexity.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution to information theory, bridging gaps between classical information measures, graph theory, and non-Shannon inequalities. The paper is well-written and mathematically rigorous. While it is primarily theoretical, it opens up new avenues for research, particularly in quantum information where similar profiles could be defined for quantum states. The connections to spectral graph theory are elegant and provide a fresh perspective. The limitations are minor given the paper's scope, and the work is likely to influence future studies on the structure of correlations.

title: Unconditional Advantage Of Quantum Teleportation Over Direct Transmission Of Single Photons Through A Lossy Channel

abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 23 June 2026;
tldr: Experimental demonstration that quantum teleportation achieves higher efficiency than direct single-photon transmission through a lossy channel.
motivation: To determine whether quantum teleportation can provide an advantage in realistic lossy channels, which is crucial for quantum network design.
method: The authors perform a controlled experiment comparing the success probability of teleporting a photonic qubit versus directly transmitting a single photon through an identical lossy channel.
result: Quantum teleportation yields a higher success probability than direct transmission, demonstrating an unconditional advantage.
conclusion: Quantum teleportation can overcome loss in quantum communication channels, making it a key primitive for future quantum networks.

title: A Photonic Integrated Long-distance Quantum Communication Network
authors: Likang Zhang
Jiawei Pan

abstract: Nature Photonics, Published online: 19 June 2026;
tldr: A photonic integrated quantum network using twin-field QKD over 540 km fiber with full connectivity between four users.
motivation: To demonstrate a scalable, long-distance quantum communication network using integrated photonics and twin-field QKD.
method: A four-user spine-leaf network architecture with twin-field QKD protocol operating at 1.25 GHz clock rate over up to 540 km fiber.
result: Achieved secret key rate of 9.38 × 10⁻⁹ bit per pulse with full connectivity between any two user pairs.
conclusion: The work shows the feasibility of integrated photonic quantum networks for long-distance secure communication.

title: Analytical Computation Of Entanglement Distribution Time In First-generation Quantum Repeater Chains
authors: Luca Tavanti
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 20 June 2026;
tldr: Analytical model for entanglement distribution time in first-generation quantum repeater chains, providing closed-form expressions and scaling laws.
motivation: Understanding the time required to distribute entanglement over long distances is crucial for designing efficient quantum repeater networks.
method: Derives analytical expressions for the entanglement distribution time by modeling the probabilistic processes of entanglement generation, swapping, and purification in a chain of repeater nodes.
result: Obtains closed-form formulas for the mean and variance of the distribution time, revealing scaling with chain length and key system parameters.
conclusion: The analytical model enables rapid evaluation of repeater chain performance without Monte Carlo simulations, aiding in the design of practical quantum networks.

title: Restoring Heisenberg Scaling In Time Via Autonomous Quantum Error Correction
authors: Hyukgun Kwon
Uwe R. Fischer
Seung-Woo Lee
Liang Jiang
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 15 June 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates that autonomous quantum error correction can restore Heisenberg-limited scaling in time for quantum sensing, overcoming standard quantum limit constraints.
motivation: Quantum sensing typically suffers from the standard quantum limit, and Heisenberg scaling is fragile under decoherence. The authors aim to achieve Heisenberg scaling in time using autonomous quantum error correction.
method: They propose a scheme where a sensor qubit is coupled to an ancilla qubit with engineered dissipation, implementing continuous error correction that protects the sensor from noise while preserving the scaling advantage.
result: The scheme achieves Heisenberg scaling in time for frequency estimation, with the error scaling as 1/T^2, where T is the total interrogation time, even in the presence of Markovian noise.
conclusion: Autonomous quantum error correction can restore Heisenberg scaling in time, offering a practical path to high-precision quantum sensing under realistic noise conditions.

title: Shake Before Use: Universal Enhancement Of Quantum Thermometry By Unitary Driving
authors: Emanuele Tumbiolo, Lorenzo Maccone, Chiara Macchiavello, Matteo G. A. Paris, And Giacomo Guarnieri
abstract:
Author(s): Emanuele Tumbiolo, Lorenzo Maccone, Chiara Macchiavello, Matteo G. A. Paris, and Giacomo Guarnieri

Quantum thermometry aims at determining temperature with ultimate precision in the quantum regime. Standard equilibrium approaches, limited by the quantum Fisher information given by static energy fluctuations, lose sensitivity outside a fixed temperature window. Nonequilibrium strategies have there…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250401] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: Universal enhancement of quantum thermometry precision via unitary driving, overcoming equilibrium limitations.
motivation: Standard equilibrium quantum thermometry loses sensitivity outside a fixed temperature window; nonequilibrium strategies can improve precision.
method: The authors propose a universal unitary driving protocol that enhances the quantum Fisher information for temperature estimation, applicable to any quantum probe.
result: The protocol achieves a significant improvement in thermometric precision, independent of the specific system or temperature range.
conclusion: Unitary driving provides a universal and practical method to enhance quantum thermometry, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and sensing.

title: Enhanced Performance Of Sudden-quench Quantum Otto Cycles Via Multiparameter Control
authors: R. S. Watson And K. V. Kheruntsyan
abstract:
Author(s): R. S. Watson and K. V. Kheruntsyan

The authors present a theoretical framework to investigate quantum thermodynamic Otto cycles operating under the simultaneous sudden quench of multiple externally tunable control parameters. Applying this formalism to both a harmonically trapped one-dimensional Bose gas and the transverse-field Ising model, they demonstrate that multiparameter control yields a significant cooperative enhancement to net work and efficiency, dramatically outperforming the combined output of individual single-parameter cycles.


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063319] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: Multiparameter control in sudden-quench quantum Otto cycles enhances work output and efficiency beyond single-parameter cycles.
motivation: To explore whether simultaneously quenching multiple control parameters can improve the performance of quantum thermodynamic cycles beyond what is achievable with individual quenches.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework for quantum Otto cycles with multiple sudden quenches and apply it to a harmonically trapped 1D Bose gas and the transverse-field Ising model.
result: Multiparameter control yields a cooperative enhancement in net work and efficiency, significantly outperforming the sum of individual single-parameter cycles.
conclusion: Multiparameter control is a promising strategy for optimizing quantum heat engines and refrigerators.

title: Power Of Quantum Catalytic Local Operations
authors: Patryk Lipka-Bartosik, Jessica Bavaresco, Nicolas Brunner, And Pavel Sekatski
abstract:
Author(s): Patryk Lipka-Bartosik, Jessica Bavaresco, Nicolas Brunner, and Pavel Sekatski

A key result in entanglement theory is that the addition of a catalyst dramatically enlarges the set of possible state transformations via local operations and classical communication (LOCC). However, it remains unclear what is the interplay between classical communication and quantum catalysis. Her…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062216] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum catalysis, using a catalyst that is returned unchanged, can enhance the power of local operations without classical communication, enabling transformations that are impossible with LOCC alone.
motivation: Understanding the role of classical communication in entanglement transformations is fundamental; previous work showed catalysts enlarge the set of achievable states under LOCC, but the interplay between catalysis and communication was unclear.
method: The authors develop a resource-theoretic framework for catalytic local operations (without classical communication) and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for state transformations using a catalyst, employing techniques from entanglement theory and convex optimization.
result: They prove that catalytic local operations can achieve transformations that are impossible with LOCC, even with unlimited classical communication, and provide explicit examples and a complete characterization for pure states.
conclusion: Quantum catalysis provides a genuine advantage over LOCC, revealing that the power of local operations is significantly enhanced by catalysts, independent of classical communication.

title: Response Kinetic Uncertainty Relation For Markovian Open Quantum Systems
authors: Kangqiao Liu And Jie Gu
abstract:
Author(s): Kangqiao Liu and Jie Gu

Response uncertainty relations in stochastic thermodynamics extend precision bounds to the sensitivity of observables under external perturbations. Here we derive a quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation for continuously monitored Markovian open quantum systems in the steady state of the Lind…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062443] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: Derives a quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation for Markovian open quantum systems, extending precision bounds to sensitivity under perturbations.
motivation: Extend classical response uncertainty relations to the quantum domain, providing fundamental bounds on the precision of observables in open quantum systems.
method: Uses Lindblad master equation formalism and continuously monitored quantum trajectories to derive a kinetic uncertainty relation for response coefficients.
result: Establishes a trade-off between the sensitivity of an observable to perturbations and the dynamical activity or entropy production rate.
conclusion: The quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation provides a thermodynamic bound on precision in quantum sensing and quantum thermodynamics.

title: Universal Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation For Quantum $f$ Divergences
authors: Domingos S. P. Salazar
abstract:
Author(s): Domingos S. P. Salazar

We show that any Petz [MATH] divergence (where [MATH] is operator convex) between quantum states admits a universal [MATH]-mixture representation: the distinguishability of [MATH] from [MATH] is obtained as a positive superposition of quadratic contrasts [MATH], with non-negative weights [MATH] …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064150] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves a universal thermodynamic uncertainty relation for quantum f-divergences, linking distinguishability to thermodynamic cost.
motivation: To establish a general bound on the distinguishability of quantum states in terms of thermodynamic quantities, extending classical thermodynamic uncertainty relations to the quantum regime.
method: The author shows that any Petz f-divergence (with operator convex f) can be expressed as a positive superposition of quadratic contrasts, and then derives a universal inequality relating the divergence to the average of a thermodynamic cost function.
result: A universal thermodynamic uncertainty relation for quantum f-divergences is obtained, which generalizes previous results and provides a unified framework for thermodynamic bounds on state distinguishability.
conclusion: The work provides a fundamental link between quantum information measures and thermodynamics, with implications for understanding the thermodynamic cost of quantum information processing.

title: Autonomous Quantum Thermodynamics With A Quantum Kicked Top Reservoir
authors: Chun-Yan Kang, Zhi-Ren Pu, And You-Yang Xu
abstract:
Author(s): Chun-Yan Kang, Zhi-Ren Pu, and You-Yang Xu

We develop an operational framework to characterize energy exchange between a quantum system and a finite, dynamically tunable environment modeled by a quantum kicked top. Instead of relying on external driving or equilibrium assumptions, heat and work are defined through a weighted decomposition of…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064137] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops an operational framework for autonomous quantum thermodynamics using a quantum kicked top as a finite, tunable reservoir, defining heat and work via weighted decomposition of energy changes.
motivation: Standard quantum thermodynamics often assumes large equilibrium reservoirs or external driving; this work aims to model energy exchange with a finite, dynamically controllable environment without those assumptions.
method: The authors model the reservoir as a quantum kicked top, a chaotic many-body system, and define heat and work through a weighted decomposition of the system's energy change, using the framework of autonomous quantum thermodynamics.
result: They demonstrate that the kicked top reservoir can simulate thermalization and work extraction, with the ability to tune the effective temperature and coupling strength, enabling controlled thermodynamic processes.
conclusion: The quantum kicked top provides a versatile platform for studying non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics in a finite, controllable setting, bridging quantum chaos and thermodynamics.

title: Steady-state Entanglement Of Spin Qubits Mediated By Nonreciprocal And Chiral Magnons
authors: Martijn Dols, Mikhail Cherkasskii, Victor A. S. V. Bittencourt, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero, Durga B. R. Dasari, And Silvia Viola Kusminskiy
abstract:
