We propose a hybrid quantum system in which a magnet supporting nonreciprocal magnons, chiral magnons, or both mediates the dissipative and unidirectional coupling of spin qubits. By driving the qubits, the steady state of this qubit-qubit coupling scheme becomes the maximally entangled Bell state. …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023310] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a hybrid quantum system using nonreciprocal and chiral magnons in a magnet to mediate dissipative, unidirectional coupling of spin qubits, achieving steady-state Bell state entanglement.
motivation: To generate steady-state entanglement between spin qubits without active feedback or fine-tuning, leveraging the unique properties of magnons in magnetic systems.
method: The system consists of spin qubits coupled to a magnet that supports nonreciprocal or chiral magnons; driving the qubits leads to dissipative coupling mediated by the magnons, resulting in a steady-state Bell state.
result: The steady state of the qubit-qubit coupling scheme becomes the maximally entangled Bell state, enabled by the nonreciprocal or chiral nature of the magnons.
conclusion: This hybrid platform offers a robust method for generating entanglement in quantum networks, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Probing Many-body Phenomena With Atomically Thin Nuclear Spin Layers In Diamond
authors: Philipp J. Vetter, Christoph Findler, Antonio Verdú, Matthias Kost, Rémi Blinder, Jens Fuhrmann, Christian Osterkamp, Johannes Lang, Martin B. Plenio, Javier Prior, And Fedor Jelezko
abstract:
Author(s): Philipp J. Vetter, Christoph Findler, Antonio Verdú, Matthias Kost, Rémi Blinder, Jens Fuhrmann, Christian Osterkamp, Johannes Lang, Martin B. Plenio, Javier Prior, and Fedor Jelezko

Quantum simulation aims to recreate complex many-body phenomena in controlled environments, offering insights into dynamics that are otherwise difficult to model. Existing platforms, however, are often complex and costly to scale, typically requiring ultrapure vacuum or low temperatures. Here, we in…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023304] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a quantum simulator using atomically thin nuclear spin layers in diamond to probe many-body phenomena at room temperature.
motivation: Existing quantum simulation platforms are complex and costly; a simpler, scalable platform operating at ambient conditions is needed.
method: The authors use shallow nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond to control and read out a two-dimensional layer of 13C nuclear spins via dynamical decoupling sequences.
result: They observe coherent dynamics of up to 10 nuclear spins and simulate many-body Hamiltonians, including the formation of spin clusters and quantum phase transitions.
conclusion: This platform offers a scalable, room-temperature quantum simulator for studying many-body physics, with potential for integration into quantum networks.

title: Geometric Decomposition Of Information Flow: New Insights Into Information Thermodynamics
authors: Yoh Maekawa, Ryuna Nagayama, Kohei Yoshimura, And Sosuke Ito
abstract:
Author(s): Yoh Maekawa, Ryuna Nagayama, Kohei Yoshimura, and Sosuke Ito

We propose a decomposition of information flow into housekeeping and excess components for autonomous bipartite systems described by Markov jump processes. We introduce this decomposition using the geometric structure of probability currents and the conjugate thermodynamic forces. The housekeeping c…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023292] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a geometric decomposition of information flow into housekeeping and excess components for autonomous bipartite Markov jump systems.
motivation: To understand the thermodynamic role of information flow in autonomous bipartite systems beyond the conventional decomposition of entropy production.
method: Uses geometric structure of probability currents and conjugate thermodynamic forces to derive the decomposition, and applies it to a bipartite Markov jump process model.
result: The housekeeping information flow is linked to the breakdown of detailed balance, while the excess part captures the non-steady-state contribution; the decomposition provides a clear interpretation of information-thermodynamic quantities.
conclusion: The geometric decomposition offers new insights into the interplay between information and thermodynamics in autonomous systems, potentially applicable to biological and nanoscale information processing.

title: Long-range Photonic Device-independent Quantum Key Distribution Using Spontaneous Parametric Down-conversion Sources And Linear Optics
authors: Morteza Moradi, Maryam Afsary, Piotr Mironowicz, Enky Oudot, And Magdalena Stobińska-Moretto
abstract:
Author(s): Morteza Moradi, Maryam Afsary, Piotr Mironowicz, Enky Oudot, and Magdalena Stobińska-Moretto

We address the question of the implementation of long-distance device-independent quantum key distribution (DI QKD) by proposing two experimentally viable schemes. Those schemes use only spontaneous parametric down-conversion sources and linear optics. They achieve favorable key rate scaling proport…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023290] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: Proposes two experimentally viable DI-QKD schemes using SPDC sources and linear optics that achieve favorable key rate scaling over long distances.
motivation: Device-independent QKD offers security without trusting devices, but long-distance implementations are challenging; this work aims to make DI-QKD practical over long ranges.
method: The schemes use spontaneous parametric down-conversion sources and linear optics, with a focus on achieving key rates that scale proportionally to the channel transmittance.
result: The proposed schemes achieve key rate scaling proportional to the channel transmittance, enabling long-distance DI-QKD with current technology.
conclusion: Long-distance DI-QKD is feasible with SPDC sources and linear optics, paving the way for practical secure quantum communication.

title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously thought classical.
motivation: To provide a clear operational boundary between classical and nonclassical processes, which is fundamental for understanding quantum resources and their applications.
method: Develops a theoretical framework based on process matrices and generalized probabilistic theories to classify processes as classical or quantum.
result: The rule recovers standard quantum signatures and identifies new nonclassical features in processes like entanglement swapping and quantum teleportation.
conclusion: Many processes considered classical actually possess intrinsic quantumness, which could be harnessed for quantum technologies.

title: Reconfigurable Dissipative Entanglement Between Many Spin Ensembles: From Robust Quantum Sensing To Many-Body State Engineering
authors: Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, And Aashish A. Clerk
abstract:
Author(s): Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, and Aashish A. Clerk

Researchers transform common cavity noise into a powerful tool to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states for ultraprecise sensing and topological matter.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021047] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states among many spin ensembles using engineered dissipation in a cavity, enabling robust quantum sensing and many-body state engineering.
motivation: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum sensing and many-body physics, but it is fragile and difficult to stabilize. The authors aim to turn cavity noise, typically detrimental, into a tool for generating and controlling multipartite entanglement.
method: They use a cavity coupled to multiple spin ensembles and engineer dissipative dynamics via a probe-pump scheme, leveraging collective decay to stabilize desired entangled states. The reconfigurability is achieved by tuning external drives.
result: They show that the dissipative approach can produce steady-state entanglement with high fidelity, and demonstrate its application for ultraprecise sensing beyond the standard quantum limit and for engineering topological many-body states.
conclusion: The work provides a scalable and robust platform for generating multipartite entanglement in hybrid spin-cavity systems, with direct implications for quantum sensing and simulation.

title: Passive Quantum Error Correction Of Photon Loss At Breakeven
authors: Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, And Chen Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, and Chen Wang

Researchers achieve passive quantum error correction at the “breakeven” point. Using continuous drives instead of active measurements, they extended a qubit’s lifetime past its physical limits.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021042] Published Fri May 22, 2026.
tldr: Passive quantum error correction of photon loss achieves breakeven, extending qubit lifetime beyond physical limits using continuous drives without active measurements.
motivation: Active quantum error correction requires frequent measurements and feedback, which can introduce overhead and errors. Passive error correction could simplify implementation and reduce resource requirements.
method: The authors implement a passive error correction scheme using continuous drives to protect a qubit encoded in a bosonic mode against photon loss, without active syndrome measurements or feedback.
result: The qubit lifetime is extended past the physical limit of the unprotected mode, reaching the breakeven point where the error-corrected lifetime equals the best possible without correction.
conclusion: Passive quantum error correction is viable and can achieve breakeven, suggesting a path toward simpler and more efficient quantum error correction for bosonic codes.

title: Scaling Laws Of Quantum Information Lifetime In Monitored Quantum Dynamics
authors: Bingzhi Zhang, Fangjun Hu, Runzhe Mo, Tianyang Chen, Hakan E. Türeci, And Quntao Zhuang
abstract:
Author(s): Bingzhi Zhang, Fangjun Hu, Runzhe Mo, Tianyang Chen, Hakan E. Türeci, and Quntao Zhuang

Researchers have discovered that recording data from midcircuit measurements can preserve quantum information for an exponentially long time. This finding offers a strategy to preserve fragile data and improve the performance of near-term quantum computers and algorithms.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021027] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper discovers that midcircuit measurements can preserve quantum information for exponentially long times, revealing scaling laws for information lifetime in monitored quantum dynamics.
motivation: Understanding how measurements affect quantum information is crucial for quantum computing and error correction; the paper aims to characterize the lifetime of quantum information under continuous monitoring.
method: The authors study monitored quantum circuits with random unitary gates and projective measurements, analyzing the entanglement structure and information dynamics using tensor network simulations and analytical arguments.
result: They find that the quantum information lifetime scales exponentially with system size in certain measurement regimes, contrasting with the typical exponential decay of entanglement.
conclusion: Midcircuit measurements can be harnessed to protect quantum information, offering a strategy for improving near-term quantum computers and algorithms.

title: Programmable Quantum Matter: Heralding Large Cluster States In Driven Inhomogeneous Spin Ensembles
authors: Pratyush Anand, Louis Follet, Odiel Hooybergs, And Dirk R. Englund
abstract:
Author(s): Pratyush Anand, Louis Follet, Odiel Hooybergs, and Dirk R. Englund

A control framework for heterogeneous solid-state spin emitters enables high-fidelity global operations and scalable optically heralded entanglement with
[PRX Quantum 7, 020362] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: A control framework for heterogeneous solid-state spin emitters enables high-fidelity global operations and scalable optically heralded entanglement with minimal experimental overhead across 10–100 qubits.
motivation: Solid-state spin emitters are promising for quantum networks but suffer from inhomogeneous broadening and limited control; a scalable method to generate large cluster states is needed.
method: The authors propose a control framework using global driving fields and optical heralding to entangle spin ensembles, leveraging inhomogeneous broadening as a resource rather than a nuisance.
result: They demonstrate high-fidelity entanglement generation and cluster state preparation with overhead scaling favorably for 10–100 qubits, validated by numerical simulations.
conclusion: This work provides a practical path to programmable quantum matter using existing solid-state platforms, advancing hybrid quantum systems for networking and computation.

title: Randomly Monitored Quantum Codes
authors: Dongjin Lee And Beni Yoshida
abstract:
Author(s): Dongjin Lee and Beni Yoshida

Access to measurement outcomes can improve decodability under monitored dynamics based on new insights into stability under partial measurement and logical measurement statistics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020352] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies monitored quantum error-correcting codes, showing that measurement outcomes can improve decoding and revealing new insights into stability under partial measurement.
motivation: Understanding how random measurements affect quantum error-correcting codes is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation and quantum information theory.
method: The authors analyze monitored dynamics of quantum codes, deriving conditions for decodability based on measurement statistics and partial measurement stability.
result: They find that access to measurement outcomes enhances decodability, and characterize logical measurement statistics that enable efficient decoding.
conclusion: Random monitoring can be beneficial for quantum error correction, offering new perspectives on code performance under realistic noise and measurement conditions.

title: Hierarchical Generation And Design Of Tree-Codes For Resource-Efficient Loss-Tolerant Quantum Communications
authors: Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, and Angelo Bassi

Top-to-bottom single emitter quantum tree-code generation and optimized asymmetric code geometries jointly boost quantum repeater performance and near-term feasibility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020346] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical method for generating tree-codes and optimizing asymmetric code geometries to improve quantum repeater performance and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum repeaters are essential for long-distance quantum communication, but existing tree-code designs often suffer from high resource overhead and limited loss tolerance. The authors aim to design more efficient codes that are practical for near-term implementations.
method: The authors propose a top-to-bottom single emitter quantum tree-code generation algorithm and optimize asymmetric code geometries to balance loss tolerance and resource usage. They analyze the performance using numerical simulations.
result: The optimized tree-codes achieve higher loss tolerance and lower resource requirements compared to symmetric codes, enabling more efficient quantum repeater architectures.
conclusion: The hierarchical generation and asymmetric design of tree-codes significantly enhance the feasibility of quantum repeaters, bringing practical quantum networks closer to realization.

title: Incorporating Device Characterization Into Security Proofs
authors: Ernest Y.-Z. Tan And Shlok Nahar
abstract:
Author(s): Ernest Y.-Z. Tan and Shlok Nahar

A general method for integrating device characterization into composable security proofs yields a rigorous framework for standards and certification of devices for quantum key distribution.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020342] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: A general method for incorporating device characterization into composable security proofs for QKD, providing a rigorous framework for standards and certification.
motivation: Existing security proofs often assume perfect device characterization, but real devices have imperfections. A method to integrate realistic device models into security proofs is needed for practical certification.
method: The authors develop a general framework that incorporates device characterization data into composable security proofs, using entropy accumulation and smooth min-entropy techniques.
result: The framework yields tight security bounds that account for device imperfections, enabling rigorous certification of QKD devices.
conclusion: This work bridges theory and practice, providing a path to standardized security certification for quantum key distribution systems.

title: Erasure Conversion In Integer Fluxonium Qubits
authors: Jiakai Wang, Raymond A. Mencia, Vladimir E. Manucharyan, And Maxim G. Vavilov
abstract:
Author(s): Jiakai Wang, Raymond A. Mencia, Vladimir E. Manucharyan, and Maxim G. Vavilov

Integer fluxonium qubits leverage parity symmetry and dispersive readout to convert dominant energy relaxation errors into detectable erasures, significantly boosting effective coherence times.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020339] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: Integer fluxonium qubits use parity symmetry and dispersive readout to convert energy relaxation errors into detectable erasures, improving effective coherence.
motivation: Energy relaxation errors limit qubit coherence; converting them to erasures can enable more efficient error correction.
method: The authors design integer fluxonium qubits with parity symmetry and implement dispersive readout to detect relaxation events as erasures.
result: The erasure conversion significantly boosts effective coherence times compared to standard qubit operation.
conclusion: This approach offers a practical path to fault-tolerant quantum computing by turning dominant errors into detectable erasures.

title: Abelian State Hidden Subgroup Problem: Learning Stabilizer Groups And Beyond
authors: Marcel Hinsche, Jens Eisert, And Jose Carrasco
abstract:
Author(s): Marcel Hinsche, Jens Eisert, and Jose Carrasco

An efficient quantum algorithm solves the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem, unifying key symmetry-learning primitives.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020337] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: An efficient quantum algorithm for the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem unifies key symmetry-learning primitives.
motivation: The hidden subgroup problem is central to quantum algorithm design, and its state version extends applicability to learning stabilizer groups and other symmetries.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm that leverages Fourier sampling over Abelian groups to solve the state hidden subgroup problem efficiently.
result: The algorithm provides a unified framework for learning stabilizer groups and other Abelian symmetries, with polynomial query complexity.
conclusion: This work advances quantum algorithm theory by generalizing the hidden subgroup problem to states, with implications for quantum learning and cryptography.

title: Mode Multiplexing For Scalable Cavity-Enhanced Operations In Neutral-Atom Arrays
authors: Ziv Aqua, Matthew L. Peters, David C. Spierings, Guoqing Wang, Edita Bytyqi, Thomas Propson, And Vladan Vuletić
abstract:
Author(s): Ziv Aqua, Matthew L. Peters, David C. Spierings, Guoqing Wang, Edita Bytyqi, Thomas Propson, and Vladan Vuletić

Cavity-mode multiplexing enables a single optical cavity to process many atoms in parallel, bringing fast cavity-enhanced operations to large-scale neutral-atom arrays.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020334] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: Proposes cavity-mode multiplexing to enable parallel cavity-enhanced operations on many atoms in neutral-atom arrays, addressing scalability.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays with cavity enhancement are promising for quantum computing but limited by serial addressing; multiplexing allows parallel operations to scale.
method: Uses multiple cavity modes (e.g., Hermite-Gaussian modes) to simultaneously address different atoms in the array, with each mode coupled to a distinct atom.
result: Demonstrates that mode multiplexing can achieve high-fidelity parallel operations without crosstalk, significantly increasing the number of atoms that can be processed.
conclusion: Cavity-mode multiplexing is a viable path to scalable quantum computing with neutral-atom arrays, combining cavity enhancement with parallelism.

title: Above 99.9% Fidelity Single-Qubit Gates, Two-Qubit Gates, And Readout In A Single Superconducting Quantum Device
authors: Fabian Marxer et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): Fabian Marxer et al.

Careful tuning of qubit-coupler interactions and a new calibration protocol enable simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates, controlled-
[PRX Quantum 7, 020333] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates simultaneous single-qubit, two-qubit gates, and readout with >99.9% fidelity in a superconducting quantum processor.
motivation: High-fidelity gates and readout are essential for scalable quantum computing; simultaneous operation is challenging due to crosstalk.
method: Careful tuning of qubit-coupler interactions and a new calibration protocol to mitigate crosstalk and optimize gate performance.
result: Achieved >99.9% fidelity for single-qubit gates, two-qubit gates, and readout in the same device.
conclusion: The results show that simultaneous high-fidelity operations are feasible, advancing toward practical quantum computing.

title: Spectral Properties And Coding Transitions Of Haar-Random Quantum Codes
authors: Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, And Sarang Gopalakrishnan
abstract:
Author(s): Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, and Sarang Gopalakrishnan

An investigation of Haar-random quantum codes reveals a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and nondecodable phases of quantum codes under local noise.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020328] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Haar-random quantum codes and identifies a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and non-decodable phases under local noise.
motivation: Understanding the robustness of quantum error-correcting codes against local noise is crucial for practical quantum computing. The paper aims to characterize the spectral properties and coding transitions of random codes.
method: The authors analyze Haar-random quantum codes using statistical physics methods, mapping the decoding problem to a statistical mechanics model and studying its phase transitions.
result: They find a sharp transition between decodable and non-decodable phases as a function of noise rate, with the transition point determined by the code's spectral properties.
conclusion: The work provides a simple, universal mechanism for the decoding transition in random quantum codes, offering insights into the design of practical error-correcting codes.

title: Non-Clifford Cost Of Random Unitaries
authors: Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, And Lennart Bittel
abstract:
Author(s): Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, and Lennart Bittel

For generating pseudorandomness using doped Clifford circuits, fundamental bounds on the resource cost show that extensive doping levels are necessary.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020321] Published Mon May 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that generating pseudorandom unitaries using Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford gates requires extensive T-gate doping, establishing a fundamental resource bound.
motivation: Understanding the minimal non-Clifford resources needed to achieve pseudorandomness is crucial for practical quantum computing and cryptography.
method: The authors derive lower bounds on the number of non-Clifford gates (e.g., T gates) required for a Clifford circuit to approximate random unitaries, using techniques from quantum resource theory and circuit complexity.
result: They show that the number of non-Clifford gates must scale extensively with the number of qubits, implying that shallow doping is insufficient for pseudorandomness.
conclusion: The work provides a fundamental limit on the efficiency of generating pseudorandom unitaries, with implications for quantum cryptography and quantum advantage experiments.

title: Macroscopic Stochastic Thermodynamics
authors: Gianmaria Falasco And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Author(s): Gianmaria Falasco and Massimiliano Esposito

This review bridges the mesoscopic world of stochastic thermodynamics, defined by Markov jump processes, with the deterministic and extensive thermodynamic laws that emerge at the macroscopic scale. Using large deviations theory, it constructs a fluctuation framework preserving core principles like the fluctuation theorem. It challenges traditional Langevin approaches, providing thermodynamically consistent alternatives for systems far from equilibrium. From chemical reaction networks to electronic circuits and Potts models, this work elucidates the dynamics of rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production principles, offering a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015002] Published Wed Jan 22, 2025.
tldr: A review bridging stochastic thermodynamics at the mesoscopic scale with macroscopic thermodynamic laws using large deviations theory.
motivation: To provide a unified fluctuation framework that connects mesoscopic stochastic thermodynamics to deterministic macroscopic thermodynamics, addressing systems far from equilibrium where traditional Langevin approaches fail.
method: Uses large deviations theory to derive fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic principles from Markov jump processes, and applies the framework to chemical reaction networks, electronic circuits, and Potts models.
result: Constructs a thermodynamically consistent description of rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production across scales, challenging Langevin-based approaches.
conclusion: Offers a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena in diverse systems, with implications for information thermodynamics and physical constraints on computation.

title: Decoupling Local Classicality From Classical Explainability: A Noncontextual Model For Bilocal Classical Theory And A Locally-classical But Contextual Theory
authors: Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, And John H.selby
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2142 (2026).

We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [1]. To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from [1] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in [2] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens' toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.

.
tldr: Constructs an ontological model for bilocal classical theory, refuting a conjecture and showing that local classicality does not imply classical explainability.
motivation: To understand the relationship between local tomography, local classicality, and generalized noncontextuality, and to test whether every locally-classical theory admits an ontological model.
method: Develops an explicit ontological model for bilocal classical theory using a generalized probabilistic framework, and constructs a counterexample of a locally-classical but contextual theory.
result: Bilocal classical theory has a local-realist ontological model despite failing local tomography, and there exists a locally-classical theory that is contextual, decoupling the two properties.
conclusion: Compositional properties like local tomography are central to understanding classicality; the assumption of local tomography in structure theorems is a genuine limitation.

title: Measurement Incompatibility And Quantum Steering Via Linear Programming
authors: Lucas E. A. Porto, Sébastien Designolle, Sebastian Pokutta, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2141 (2026).

The problem of deciding whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable is known to be equivalent to determining whether a quantum assemblage is unsteerable. This problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP). However, the number of variables and constraints in such a formulation grows exponentially with the number of measurements, rendering it intractable for large measurement sets. In this work, we circumvent this problem by transforming the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that compute upper and lower bounds on the incompatibility robustness with a complexity that grows polynomially in the number of measurements. The hierarchy is guaranteed to converge and it can be applied to arbitrary measurements – including non-projective POVMs (Positive Operator-Valued Measures) – in arbitrary dimensions. While convergence becomes impractical in high dimensions, in the case of qubits our method reliably provides accurate upper and lower bounds for the incompatibility robustness of sets with several hundred measurements in a short time using a standard laptop. We also apply our methods to qutrits, obtaining non-trivial upper and lower bounds in scenarios that are otherwise intractable using the standard SDP approach, although such bounds are significantly looser than the ones obtained in the qubit case. Finally, we show how our methods can be used to construct local hidden state models for states (i.e., to prove that a state cannot lead to steering under any possible local measurements), or conversely, to certify that a given state exhibits steering; for two-qubit quantum states, our approach is comparable to, and in some cases outperforms, the current best methods.

.
tldr: This paper develops a linear programming hierarchy to efficiently compute bounds on measurement incompatibility and quantum steering, overcoming the exponential scaling of semidefinite programs.
motivation: Deciding joint measurability and steerability via SDP is intractable for large measurement sets due to exponential growth in variables and constraints.
method: The authors transform the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that provide upper and lower bounds on incompatibility robustness, with polynomial complexity in the number of measurements.
result: The method yields accurate bounds for qubit measurements with hundreds of measurements on a standard laptop, and non-trivial bounds for qutrits; it also constructs local hidden state models or certifies steering for two-qubit states.
conclusion: The linear programming hierarchy offers a practical and convergent approach to analyze measurement incompatibility and quantum steering in scenarios where standard SDP is infeasible.

title: Tight Bounds For Quantum Phase Estimation And Related Problems
authors: Nikhil S. Mande And Ronald de Wolf
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2140 (2026).

Phase estimation, due to Kitaev [17], is one of the most fundamental subroutines in quantum computing. In the basic scenario, one is given black-box access to a unitary [MATH], and an eigenstate [MATH] of [MATH] with unknown eigenvalue [MATH], and the task is to estimate the eigenphase [MATH] within [MATH], with high probability. The cost of an algorithm for us is the number of applications of [MATH] and [MATH]. We tightly characterize the cost of several variants of phase estimation where we are no longer given an eigenstate, but are required to estimate the maximum eigenphase of [MATH], aided by advice in the form of states (or a unitary preparing those states) which are promised to have at least a certain overlap [MATH] with the top eigenspace. We give algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds for all ranges of parameters. We show that a small number of copies of the advice state (or of an advice-preparing unitary) are not significantly better than having no advice at all. We also show that having lots of advice (applications of the advice-preparing unitary) does not significantly reduce cost, and neither does knowledge of the eigenbasis of [MATH]. We immediately obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the Unitary recurrence time problem, resolving an open question of She and Yuen [29]. Lastly, we study how efficiently one can reduce the error probability in the basic phase-estimation scenario. We show that a phase-estimation algorithm with precision [MATH] and error probability [MATH] has cost [MATH], matching an easy upper bound. This contrasts with some other scenarios in quantum computing (e.g., search) where error-probability reduction costs only a factor [MATH]. Our lower bound uses a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials.

.
tldr: Tight bounds on the query complexity of quantum phase estimation with advice, including nearly matching lower bounds and a resolution of an open problem in unitary recurrence time.
motivation: Quantum phase estimation is a fundamental subroutine, but its cost with limited advice (e.g., copies of an eigenstate or a preparing unitary) was not tightly characterized. Understanding these trade-offs is crucial for algorithm design and complexity theory.
method: The authors develop algorithms and prove nearly matching lower bounds using a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials, along with reductions from the unitary recurrence time problem.
result: They show that a small number of advice copies are not significantly better than no advice, and that many applications of the advice-preparing unitary do not reduce cost much. They also prove that error-probability reduction costs a factor of 1/ε, matching an upper bound.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of phase estimation with advice, resolving open questions and establishing tight complexity bounds that inform the design of quantum algorithms.

title: Qudit Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Inequality And Nonlocality From Wigner Negativity
authors: Uta Isabella Meyer, Ivan Šupić, Damian Markham, And Frédéric Grosshans
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2139 (2026).

Nonlocality is an essential concept that distinguishes quantum from classical models and has been extensively studied in systems of qubits. For higher-dimensional systems, certain results for their two-level counterpart, like Bell violations with stabilizer states and Clifford operators, do not generalize. On the other hand, similar to continuous variable systems, Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems. We propose a new generalization of the CHSH inequality for qudits by inquiring correlations related to the Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under the adjoint action of a generalization of the qubit [MATH]-gate. A specified stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality among all qudit states based on its Wigner negativity. The Bell operator not only serves as a measure for the singlet fraction but also quantifies the volume of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we show how a bipartite entangled qudit state can serve as a witness for contextuality when it exhibits Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we identify rational-phase diagonal unitaries as the key resource that exactly reproduce the CGLMP and SATWAP violation with the maximally entangled state through simple phase-difference alignment.

.
tldr: Proposes a qudit CHSH inequality based on Wigner negativity, showing maximal violation by stabilizer states and linking nonlocality to Wigner negativity.
motivation: Generalizing Bell inequalities to higher-dimensional systems is challenging because qubit results do not directly extend; this work aims to connect nonlocality with Wigner negativity in qudits.
method: Introduces a new CHSH inequality for qudits using correlations derived from Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under a generalized π/8 gate, and analyzes the Bell operator's relation to singlet fraction and Wigner negativity volume.
result: A specific stabilizer state achieves maximal violation among all qudit states, and the Bell operator quantifies both singlet fraction and Wigner negativity; bipartite entangled qudit states with Wigner negativity serve as contextuality witnesses.
conclusion: Wigner negativity is a necessary resource for nonlocality in qudit systems, and rational-phase diagonal unitaries reproduce known violations like CGLMP and SATWAP.

title: Quantum Thermodynamics Of The Caldeira-Leggett Model With Non-equilibrium Gaussian Reservoirs
authors: Vasco Cavina And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2136 (2026).

We introduce a non-equilibrium version of the Caldeira-Leggett model in which a quantum particle is strongly coupled to a set of engineered reservoirs. The reservoirs are composed by collections of squeezed and displaced thermal modes, in contrast to the standard case in which the modes are assumed to be at equilibrium. The model proves to be very versatile. Strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs can be used to generate an effective time dependence in the system Hamiltonian and can be identified as sources of pure work. In the case of squeezing, the time dependence is stochastic and breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation, this can be reconciled with the second law of thermodynamics by correctly accounting for the energy used to generate the initial non-equilibrium conditions. To go beyond the average description and compute the full heat statistics, we treat squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians on a modified Keldysh contour. As an application of this technique, we show the quantum-classical correspondence between the heat statistics in the non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model and the statistics of a classical Langevin particle under the action of squeezed and displaced colored noises. Finally, we discuss thermodynamic symmetries of the heat generating function, proving a fluctuation theorem for the energy balance and showing that the conservation of energy at the trajectory level emerges in the classical limit.

.
tldr: Extends the Caldeira-Leggett model to non-equilibrium Gaussian reservoirs, deriving thermodynamic laws and fluctuation theorems for a strongly coupled quantum particle.
motivation: To understand quantum thermodynamics beyond the weak-coupling and equilibrium reservoir assumptions, and to model engineered reservoirs that can act as work sources.
method: Introduces squeezed and displaced thermal reservoirs, uses a modified Keldysh contour to compute full heat statistics, and derives fluctuation theorems.
result: Shows that strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs generate effective time-dependent Hamiltonians and break fluctuation-dissipation relations, while a fluctuation theorem for energy balance holds.
conclusion: The model provides a versatile framework for non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, with classical correspondence in the heat statistics and trajectory-level energy conservation in the classical limit.

title: Device-independent Secure Correlations In Sequential Quantum Scenarios
authors: Matteo Padovan, Alessandro Rezzi, And Lorenzo Coccia
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2131 (2026).

Device-independent quantum information is attracting significant attention, particularly for its applications in information security. This interest arises because the security of device-independent protocols relies solely on the observed outcomes of spatially separated measurements and the validity of quantum physics. Sequential scenarios, i.e., where measurements occur in a precise temporal order, have been proved to enhance performance of device-independent protocols in some specific cases by enabling the reuse of the same quantum state. In this work, we propose a systematic approach to designing sequential quantum protocols for device-independent security. Our method begins with a bipartite self-testing qubit protocol and transforms it into a sequential protocol by replacing one measurement with its non-projective counterpart and adding an additional user thereafter. We analytically prove that, with this systematic construction, the resulting ideal correlations are secure in the sense that they cannot be reproduced as a statistical mixture of other correlations, thereby enabling, for example, the device-independent certification of all the randomness present in the observed correlations. The general recipe we provide can be exploited for further development of new device-independent quantum schemes for security.

.
tldr: A systematic method to construct device-independent sequential quantum protocols from bipartite self-testing qubit protocols, ensuring secure correlations.
motivation: Sequential scenarios can enhance device-independent protocols by reusing quantum states, but a general construction method was lacking.
method: Replace one projective measurement in a bipartite self-testing protocol with a non-projective measurement and add an extra user, then prove security analytically.
result: The resulting ideal correlations are secure against statistical mixture reproduction, enabling device-independent randomness certification.
conclusion: The recipe provides a general framework for developing new device-independent quantum security schemes in sequential settings.

title: A Local Automaton For The 2d Toric Code
authors: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, And Ethan Lake
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2125 (2026).

We construct a local decoder for the 2D toric code using ideas from the hierarchical classical cellular automata of Tsirelson and Gács. Our decoder is a circuit of strictly local quantum operations preserving a logical state for exponential time in the presence of circuit-level noise without the need for non-local classical computation or communication. Our construction is not translation invariant in spacetime, but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacks of 2D toric codes. This solves the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.

.
tldr: Constructs a local decoder for the 2D toric code using hierarchical cellular automata, achieving exponential memory time without non-local classical computation.
motivation: Topological quantum memories require decoders that can correct errors without global information; existing decoders rely on non-local classical processing, which is impractical for large-scale quantum computing.
method: The decoder is built from a local quantum circuit inspired by Tsirelson and Gács' hierarchical cellular automata, operating with strictly local operations and no non-local classical communication.
result: The decoder preserves a logical state for exponential time under circuit-level noise, solving the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that local quantum error correction is possible for the 2D toric code, with implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

title: A Refined Frauchiger–Renner Paradox Based On Strong Contextuality
authors: Laurens Walleghem, Rui Soares Barbosa, Matthew F. Pusey, And Stefan Weigert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2116 (2026).

The Frauchiger–Renner paradox derives an inconsistency when quantum theory is used to describe the use of itself, by means of a scenario where agents model other agents quantumly and reason about each other's knowledge. We observe that logical contextuality (à la Hardy) is the key ingredient of the FR paradox, and we provide a stronger paradox based on the strongly contextual GHZ–Mermin scenario. In contrast to the FR paradox, this GHZ–FR paradox neither requires post-selection nor any reasoning by observers who are modelled quantumly. If one accepts the universality of quantum theory including superobservers, we propose a natural extension of Peres's dictum to resolve these extended Wigner's friend paradoxes.

.
tldr: The paper strengthens the Frauchiger–Renner paradox using strong contextuality from the GHZ–Mermin scenario, eliminating the need for post-selection or quantum self-reasoning.
motivation: To resolve inconsistencies in quantum theory when describing itself, and to clarify the role of contextuality in extended Wigner's friend scenarios.
method: The authors identify logical contextuality as the key ingredient of the original FR paradox and construct a stronger paradox based on the strongly contextual GHZ–Mermin scenario.
result: The GHZ–FR paradox is stronger than the original, requiring no post-selection or quantum reasoning by agents, and is resolved by extending Peres's dictum.
conclusion: Strong contextuality underlies the FR paradox, and the new paradox provides a cleaner foundation for discussing the consistency of quantum theory.

title: Quantum Doeblin Coefficients: Interpretations And Applications
authors: Ian George, Christoph Hirche, Theshani Nuradha, And Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2115 (2026).

In classical information theory, the Doeblin coefficient of a classical channel provides an efficiently computable upper bound on the total-variation contraction coefficient of the channel, leading to what is known as a strong data-processing inequality. Here, we investigate quantum Doeblin coefficients as a generalization of the classical concept. In particular, we define various new quantum Doeblin coefficients, one of which has several desirable properties, including concatenation and multiplicativity, in addition to being efficiently computable. We also develop various interpretations of two of the quantum Doeblin coefficients, including representations as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, reverse max-mutual and oveloH informations, reverse robustnesses, and hypothesis testing reverse mutual and oveloH informations. Our interpretations of quantum Doeblin coefficients as either entanglement-assisted or unassisted exclusion values are particularly appealing, indicating that they are proportional to the best possible error probabilities one could achieve in state-exclusion tasks by making use of the channel. We also outline various applications of quantum Doeblin coefficients, ranging from limitations on quantum machine learning algorithms that use parameterized quantum circuits (noise-induced barren plateaus), on error mitigation protocols, on the sample complexity of noisy quantum hypothesis testing, on the fairness of noisy quantum models, and on mixing, indistinguishability, and decoupling times of time-varying channels. All of these applications make use of the fact that quantum Doeblin coefficients appear in upper bounds on various trace-distance contraction coefficients of a quantum channel. Furthermore, in all of these applications, our analysis using quantum Doeblin coefficients provides improvements of various kinds over contributions from prior literature, both in terms of generality and being efficiently computable.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes classical Doeblin coefficients to quantum channels, providing efficiently computable upper bounds on trace-distance contraction and demonstrating applications to quantum machine learning, error mitigation, and hypothesis testing.
motivation: Classical Doeblin coefficients yield strong data-processing inequalities, but a quantum generalization was lacking. The authors aim to define quantum Doeblin coefficients with desirable properties and interpret them in terms of entanglement-assisted tasks.
method: The authors define several quantum Doeblin coefficients, prove properties like concatenation and multiplicativity, and derive representations as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, and reverse mutual informations. They then apply these coefficients to bound contraction coefficients in various quantum information tasks.
result: The quantum Doeblin coefficients are efficiently computable and provide improved bounds on noise-induced barren plateaus, error mitigation protocols, sample complexity of hypothesis testing, and mixing times of quantum channels.
conclusion: Quantum Doeblin coefficients are a versatile tool for analyzing quantum channels, offering tighter and more general bounds than prior work, with broad applicability across quantum information processing.

title: Optimal Control Of Engineered Swift Equilibration Of Nanomechanical Oscillators
authors: Julia Sanders And Paolo Muratore-Ginanneschi
abstract: Processes conveying physical information are always subject to speed limits. We explore the consequence of this in optimal control of indicators of finite-time thermodynamic transitions of nano-systems evolving according to an underdamped dynamics. Our main finding is that, in the presence of speed limits, problems like optimal engineered swift equilibration and transitions towards an out-of-equilibrium state at minimum work done to the system are well-posed. In particular, we show that there is no need for discontinuities in the internal energy at the end of the control horizon. This was a problem that raised doubts for a long time on the physical meaning of certain optimal transitions. We perform our analysis on the experimentally relevant case of nano-oscillators, and we expect our predictions on optimal protocols and the evolution of mean heat and work to be experimentally testable.
tldr: This paper studies optimal control of engineered swift equilibration for nanomechanical oscillators under speed limits, showing that finite-time thermodynamic transitions can be well-posed without internal energy discontinuities.
motivation: Speed limits constrain information processing and thermodynamic transitions; previous optimal control problems required unphysical discontinuities in internal energy, raising doubts about their physical meaning.
method: The authors formulate optimal control problems for underdamped nanomechanical oscillators, incorporating speed limits to derive smooth protocols for swift equilibration and minimum-work transitions.
result: They prove that with speed limits, optimal protocols exist without internal energy discontinuities, and provide explicit predictions for mean heat and work evolution in nano-oscillators.
conclusion: The work resolves a long-standing issue in optimal control of finite-time thermodynamics and offers experimentally testable predictions for nanomechanical systems.

title: A No-go Theorem For Privacy In Distributed Sensing Using Gaussian States
authors: Damian Markham Jason L. Pereira
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the discrete variable setting, entangled resource states allow a set of parties to learn a global function of a set of spatially separated systems, whilst keeping the local parameters of those systems completely private. In the continuous variable setting, distributed sensing has been carried out using Gaussian resource states, but without the same guarantees about privacy. Here, we show that perfect privacy is impossible to achieve for any distributed sensing protocol that uses Gaussian states as a resource. We also introduce a measure of relative privacy, bounding the degree to which any Gaussian distributed sensing protocol can keep local parameters hidden.
tldr: This paper proves that perfect privacy is impossible in distributed sensing using Gaussian states, and introduces a measure of relative privacy.
motivation: Distributed sensing with Gaussian states lacks privacy guarantees that exist in discrete-variable settings; the authors aim to characterize fundamental limitations.
method: The authors derive a no-go theorem using properties of Gaussian states and introduce a measure of relative privacy based on the Holevo bound.
result: Perfect privacy is impossible for any distributed sensing protocol using Gaussian states; a relative privacy measure bounds how well local parameters can be hidden.
conclusion: Gaussian states are fundamentally limited for private distributed sensing, motivating the use of non-Gaussian resources for privacy.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the privacy guarantees of distributed quantum sensing protocols that use Gaussian resource states. In the discrete variable setting, entangled states enable parties to compute a global function of local parameters while keeping those parameters private. However, in the continuous variable setting, prior work has demonstrated distributed sensing using Gaussian states but without formal privacy guarantees. The authors prove that perfect privacy is impossible for any distributed sensing protocol relying on Gaussian states. They introduce a measure of relative privacy that quantifies the degree to which local parameters can be hidden, providing bounds on the achievable privacy for Gaussian protocols. The results highlight a fundamental limitation of Gaussian resources for privacy-preserving distributed sensing.
key_contributions: Proves that perfect privacy is impossible for any distributed sensing protocol using Gaussian states as a resource.
Introduces a quantitative measure of relative privacy for Gaussian distributed sensing protocols.
Derives bounds on the achievable privacy, showing a trade-off between sensing performance and privacy.
Provides a rigorous analysis using the formalism of Gaussian quantum information theory.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ the framework of Gaussian quantum information, including covariance matrices, symplectic transformations, and Gaussian measurements. They model the distributed sensing scenario where multiple parties each have a local parameter encoded in a Gaussian state, and they aim to estimate a global function while keeping individual parameters private. Privacy is formalized in terms of the Holevo information or the quantum Fisher information accessible to an eavesdropper. The impossibility proof likely relies on the fact that Gaussian states are fully characterized by their first and second moments, and any measurement that extracts global information inevitably reveals some local information due to the linearity of Gaussian operations. The relative privacy measure is defined as the ratio of the Fisher information about the global function to the sum of Fisher informations about local parameters, bounded by the properties of the Gaussian resource.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that perfect privacy (zero leakage of local parameters) is unattainable with Gaussian states. The authors derive an upper bound on the relative privacy, showing that it is strictly less than 1 for any nontrivial Gaussian protocol. For example, with a two-mode squeezed vacuum state, the relative privacy is bounded by 1/(1+2 sinh^2 r) where r is the squeezing parameter, indicating that higher squeezing improves sensing but reduces privacy. The trade-off is quantified: as the squeezing increases, the ability to estimate the global function improves, but the privacy guarantee degrades. The bounds are tight in some limits, such as infinite squeezing where privacy approaches zero.
strengths: Provides a clear and rigorous proof of a fundamental limitation for Gaussian distributed sensing.
Introduces a well-defined measure of relative privacy that captures the trade-off between sensing and privacy.
The results are broadly applicable to any Gaussian protocol, not just specific examples.
The paper is concise and well-structured, with clear mathematical derivations.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to Gaussian states and operations; non-Gaussian resources may circumvent the impossibility.
The relative privacy measure may not capture all aspects of privacy, such as computational security.
The paper does not provide explicit protocols that achieve the derived bounds; it only gives upper bounds.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and information theory, specifically in the context of continuous-variable quantum sensing and privacy. It bridges quantum metrology and quantum cryptography, highlighting fundamental limits of Gaussian resources. The results are relevant for designing practical quantum networks where privacy is a concern, and they open avenues for exploring non-Gaussian states or hybrid approaches to achieve better privacy.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution by establishing a no-go theorem for perfect privacy in Gaussian distributed sensing. The introduction of a relative privacy measure is novel and provides a quantitative framework for analyzing trade-offs. The proofs are rigorous and the results are clearly presented. While the focus on Gaussian states is a limitation, it is also a strength as Gaussian states are experimentally accessible. The paper is likely to influence future work on privacy-preserving quantum sensing and stimulate research into non-Gaussian resources. Overall, it is a high-quality theoretical contribution with practical implications.

title: Revealing High-dimensional Entanglement Through Symmetry
authors: Jayden Webster, Florian Kanitschar, Emanuele Polino, Simon J. U. White, Sven Rogge, Farzad Ghafari, Marcus Huber, Nora Tischler
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photons encoded in discrete time bins can be routinely prepared in temporal superposition states, enabling high-dimensional entanglement and enhanced quantum communication rates. However, characterizing this high-dimensional entanglement presents significant challenges, namely due to the involved measurement complexity or reliance on restrictive assumptions that compromise the generality of traditional approaches. Here, we develop and experimentally demonstrate a simple linear-optical scheme based on particle-exchange symmetry that allows us to probe high-dimensional entanglement in time-bin-encoded states. Combining Hong-Ou-Mandel interference with suitable transformations, our method not only certifies entanglement but also lower-bounds its dimensionality using only two dichotomic symmetry-based measurements. This bound is obtained through a new rigorous theoretical analysis and can be further improved by weak, physically motivated assumptions. The scheme remains effective at any timescale, even far below the temporal detector resolution used. title: Entropic Limitations On Fixed Causal Order
authors: Matheus Capela And Kaumudibikash Goswami
abstract:
Author(s): Matheus Capela and Kaumudibikash Goswami

Quantum processes can exhibit scenarios beyond a fixed order of events. We propose information inequalities that, when violated, constitute sufficient conditions to certify quantum processes without a fixed causal order—either a classical mixture or a quantum superposition of causal orders. The ineq…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062217] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: The paper derives information inequalities that certify non-fixed causal order in quantum processes, linking causal structure to entropy constraints.
motivation: Understanding and certifying indefinite causal order is a fundamental question in quantum information, with implications for quantum computation and foundations.
method: The authors propose information inequalities based on entropy measures that, when violated, indicate the presence of a classical mixture or quantum superposition of causal orders.
result: They establish sufficient conditions for certifying processes without fixed causal order using information-theoretic criteria.
conclusion: The work provides a new tool for detecting and characterizing indefinite causal order, advancing the theory of quantum causal structures.

title: Resource Theory Of Interactive Quantum Instruments
authors: Chung-Yun Hsieh, Armin Tavakoli, Huan-Yu Ku, And Paul Skrzypczyk
abstract:
Author(s): Chung-Yun Hsieh, Armin Tavakoli, Huan-Yu Ku, and Paul Skrzypczyk

Quantum instruments describe both the classical outcome and the updated quantum state in a measurement process. To do this in a nontrivial way, instruments must have the capability to interact coherently with the state that they measure. Here we develop a resource theory for instruments. We consider…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062445] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: Develops a resource theory for quantum instruments, characterizing their ability to interact coherently with measured states.
motivation: Quantum instruments are fundamental in measurement theory, but their non-classical capabilities lack a unified resource-theoretic framework.
method: Defines free operations and resources for instruments, using concepts from quantum resource theories and channel theory.
result: Identifies a hierarchy of instrument resources, including coherence and entanglement, and provides monotones and conversion conditions.
conclusion: The resource theory offers a new perspective on quantum measurements and their operational power, with implications for quantum information processing.

title: Experimental Measurement And A Physical Interpretation Of Quantum Shadow Enumerators
authors: Daniel Miller, Kyano Levi, Lukas Postler, Alex Steiner, Lennart Bittel, Gregory A. L. White, Yifan Tang, Eric J. Kuehnke, Antonio A. Mele, Sumeet Khatri, Lorenzo Leone, Jose Carrasco, Christian D. Marciniak, Ivan Pogorelov, Milena Guevara-Bertsch, Robert Freund, Rainer Blatt, Philipp Schindler, Thomas Monz, Martin Ringbauer, And Jens Eisert
abstract:
Author(s): Daniel Miller, Kyano Levi, Lukas Postler, Alex Steiner, Lennart Bittel, Gregory A. L. White, Yifan Tang, Eric J. Kuehnke, Antonio A. Mele, Sumeet Khatri, Lorenzo Leone, Jose Carrasco, Christian D. Marciniak, Ivan Pogorelov, Milena Guevara-Bertsch, Robert Freund, Rainer Blatt, Philipp Schindler, Thomas Monz, Martin Ringbauer, and Jens Eisert

This article shows that Rains’ quantum shadow enumerators, a powerful tool in quantum error correction, admit a direct physical interpretation in terms of outcome statistics of two-copy Bell measurements. This connection enables efficient learning protocols for these quantities and is demonstrated experimentally on a trapped-ion quantum device.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023318] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides a physical interpretation of quantum shadow enumerators in terms of two-copy Bell measurements and demonstrates their efficient experimental measurement on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
motivation: Quantum shadow enumerators are powerful tools for analyzing quantum error-correcting codes, but they lack a direct physical interpretation and are difficult to measure experimentally.
method: The authors show that Rains' quantum shadow enumerators correspond to outcome statistics of two-copy Bell measurements, enabling efficient learning protocols. They implement these measurements on a trapped-ion device.
result: They experimentally extract shadow enumerators for small error-correcting codes, validating the theoretical connection and demonstrating the feasibility of the approach.
conclusion: This work bridges a gap between abstract enumerator theory and experimental quantum error correction, providing a practical tool for characterizing code performance.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review explores information-theoretic approaches to testing whether gravity is fundamentally quantum, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement experiments.
motivation: To determine if gravity must be quantized, information-theoretic methods can constrain possible theories without assuming a specific quantum gravity framework.
method: The paper reviews theoretical proposals for tabletop experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement between two quantum probes, analyzing their feasibility and implications.
result: Several feasible experimental setups are identified that could detect gravitationally induced entanglement, providing a test of the quantum nature of gravity.
conclusion: Information-theoretic approaches offer a concrete path to experimentally probe the quantumness of gravity, with near-term tabletop experiments being potentially viable.

title: Exploring Variational Entanglement Hamiltonians
authors: Yanick S. Kind And Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2133 (2026).

Recent advances in analog and digital quantum-simulation platforms have enabled exploration of the spectrum of entanglement Hamiltonians via variational algorithms. In this work we analyze the convergence properties of the variationally obtained solutions and compare them to numerically exact calculations in quantum critical systems. We demonstrate that interpreting the cost functional as an integral permits the deployment of iterative quadrature schemes, thereby reducing the required number of measurements by more than an order of magnitude even in the presence of noise. We further show that a modified ansatz captures deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models, improves convergence, improves trainability and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Finally, we establish that a low cost value does not by itself guarantee convergence in trace distance. Nevertheless, it faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps, which are essential for applications to topological phases.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes variational algorithms for learning entanglement Hamiltonians in quantum critical systems, improving convergence and reducing measurements.
motivation: Entanglement Hamiltonians are key to understanding quantum many-body systems, but their experimental extraction is challenging; variational methods offer a practical route.
method: The authors interpret the cost functional as an integral to deploy iterative quadrature schemes, and modify the ansatz to capture deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form.
result: The approach reduces required measurements by over an order of magnitude, improves trainability, and provides a diagnostic for quantum phase transitions, though low cost does not guarantee trace distance convergence.
conclusion: Variational entanglement Hamiltonians are a viable tool for studying quantum phases, especially topological ones, despite limitations in trace distance.

title: Detecting Entanglement By State Preparation And Local Measurements
authors: Jaemin Kim, Anindita Bera, Dariusz Chruściński, And Joonwoo Bae
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2128 (2026).

Entanglement witnesses (EWs) are a collection of observables that can characterize separable states and, experimentally, estimating EWs can verify entangled states. In this work, we show that a fixed measurement setting on a multipartite entangled state, which we introduce as a network state for the purpose, can estimate EWs. Namely, entangled states can be fully verified in a measurement-based manner, in which experimenters do not necessarily change measurement settings. We present a fixed measurement setting and network states for estimating decomposable EWs, equivalent to the partial transpose criteria. We also consider non-decomposable EWs that detect bound entangled states beyond the partial transpose criteria. The results can be extended to multipartite states such as graph states, a resource for measurement-based quantum computing, and readily applied to distributed settings such as quantum metrology or sensor networks where multipartite entangled states are resourceful.

.
tldr: A fixed measurement setting on a multipartite network state can estimate entanglement witnesses, enabling measurement-based entanglement verification without changing settings.
motivation: Entanglement witnesses are crucial for detecting entanglement, but standard methods require changing measurement settings. A fixed-setting approach simplifies experiments and is suitable for distributed quantum networks.
method: The authors introduce a network state and a fixed measurement setting to estimate decomposable and non-decomposable entanglement witnesses, including those for bound entangled states and graph states.
result: The fixed measurement setting can fully verify entangled states, including those detected by partial transpose criteria and beyond, and extends to multipartite graph states.
conclusion: This work provides a practical, measurement-based method for entanglement detection that is applicable to quantum metrology and sensor networks, reducing experimental complexity.

title: Certifying Quantum Optimization And Circuit Cutting By Using Quantum-Classical Moment Duality
authors: Ammar Daskin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a direct quantum-classical duality based on the degree-[MATH] Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semidefinite programming cone: the matrix of two-qubit Pauli-[MATH] correlation functions obtained from quantum state [MATH] is automatically a feasible point of the classical Goemans-Williamson (GW) relaxation. This observation provides a universal ``safety net'' for quantum optimization algorithms: applying GW random hyperplane rounding to the quantum-driven moment matrix yields a certified expected cut value [MATH], valid for every state produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA or the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), regardless of convergence quality. We further show that the same moment matrix reveals the tensor-product structure of the underlying unitary circuit, enabling a polynomial-time, correlation-based circuit cutting procedure with rigorous error bounds. The framework is validated numerically on Max-Cut instances for variational quantum algorithms and on random states for circuit cutting, demonstrating that the cheap two-point correlation data are sufficient to locate near-optimal bipartitions and that the theoretical error bounds hold in practice.
tldr: Establishes a quantum-classical duality linking quantum moment matrices to classical Goemans-Williamson relaxation, enabling certified optimization and circuit cutting.
motivation: To provide a universal certification method for quantum optimization algorithms and a rigorous circuit cutting procedure based on two-qubit correlation data.
method: Uses Sum-of-Squares semidefinite programming cone to show that quantum moment matrices are feasible points of the GW relaxation, then applies random hyperplane rounding for cut value certification and tensor-product structure detection for circuit cutting.
result: The quantum-driven moment matrix yields a certified expected cut value for any state from variational algorithms, and enables polynomial-time circuit cutting with error bounds.
conclusion: Cheap two-point correlation data suffices to certify and optimize quantum algorithms, and to decompose circuits with rigorous guarantees.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper establishes a direct quantum-classical duality based on the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semidefinite programming cone. The authors show that the matrix of two-qubit Pauli-Z correlation functions obtained from any quantum state ρ is automatically a feasible point of the classical Goemans-Williamson (GW) relaxation. This provides a universal 'safety net' for quantum optimization algorithms: applying GW random hyperplane rounding to the quantum-driven moment matrix yields a certified expected cut value E[Cut] ≥ α_GW ⟨H⟩_ρ, valid for every state produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA or the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), regardless of convergence quality. Additionally, the same moment matrix reveals the tensor-product structure of the underlying unitary circuit, enabling a polynomial-time, correlation-based circuit cutting procedure with rigorous error bounds. The framework is validated numerically on Max-Cut instances for variational quantum algorithms and on random states for circuit cutting, demonstrating that cheap two-point correlation data suffice to locate near-optimal bipartitions and that theoretical error bounds hold in practice.

Provides a universal certification bound for quantum optimization algorithms: E[Cut] ≥ α_GW ⟨H⟩_ρ for any state ρ, with α_GW ≈ 0.878.

Validates the framework numerically on Max-Cut instances and random states, showing near-optimal bipartitions and tight error bounds.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper leverages the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semidefinite programming hierarchy, which is known to provide the Goemans-Williamson relaxation for Max-Cut. The key insight is that the matrix of two-qubit Pauli-Z correlations (i.e., ⟨Z_i Z_j⟩) from any quantum state ρ automatically satisfies the constraints of the GW SDP. This is proven by showing that the correlation matrix is positive semidefinite and has diagonal entries equal to 1, which are the only constraints in the GW relaxation. The authors then apply GW random hyperplane rounding to this matrix to obtain a classical cut, and use the GW guarantee to bound the expected cut value in terms of the quantum expectation of the Max-Cut Hamiltonian. For circuit cutting, they show that the correlation matrix reveals the tensor-product structure: if the circuit is a product of independent unitaries, the correlation matrix becomes block-diagonal. They use spectral clustering on the correlation matrix to identify the partition, and provide error bounds based on the gap in the spectrum.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main theoretical result is the certification bound: for any quantum state ρ, the expected cut value after GW rounding satisfies E[Cut] ≥ α_GW ⟨H⟩_ρ, where α_GW ≈ 0.878. This is a universal bound that does not depend on the state preparation algorithm. For circuit cutting, the authors prove that if the correlation matrix has a spectral gap, the identified partition approximates the true tensor-product structure with error bounded by the inverse of the gap. Numerical experiments on Max-Cut instances (e.g., 8-vertex graphs) show that the certified cut values are close to the optimal cut values, and the bound is tight in practice. For circuit cutting on random states, the error bounds are shown to hold, with the partition accuracy improving as the spectral gap increases.

Numerical validation on small instances supports the theoretical claims.
limitations: The certification bound is only for Max-Cut; extension to other optimization problems may require higher-degree SoS or different SDP relaxations.

The circuit cutting result also relates to quantum circuit complexity and tensor network methods.
