A comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial is shown to serve as a benchmark for quantum computers and yield new insights into potential quantum advantage.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020355] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial, serving as a benchmark for quantum computers.
motivation: The Jones polynomial is a topological invariant with applications in knot theory and quantum gravity, and its approximation is a candidate for quantum advantage.
method: The authors design an end-to-end quantum algorithm that maps the Jones polynomial evaluation to a quantum circuit, including state preparation, unitary evolution, and measurement, and implement it on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
result: They demonstrate the algorithm on small knots and links, showing agreement with classical simulations and highlighting resource requirements for scaling.
conclusion: The work establishes a practical benchmark for quantum computers and provides insights into the potential for quantum advantage in topological computations.

title: Photon Catalysis For General Multimode Multi-Photon Quantum State Preparation
authors: Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, And Massimo Frigerio
abstract:
Author(s): Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, and Massimo Frigerio

Using a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition, every photonic state can be prepared with realistic experimental tools and a predictable number of steps.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020323] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: A method for preparing arbitrary photonic states using symmetric tensor decomposition and photon catalysis.
motivation: To provide a systematic and experimentally feasible approach for generating complex multimode multi-photon quantum states.
method: The authors use symmetric tensor decomposition to decompose target states into a sequence of elementary operations, including photon catalysis and linear optics.
result: They show that any photonic state can be prepared with a predictable number of steps using realistic experimental tools.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a general and efficient recipe for photonic state preparation, advancing quantum optics experiments.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge in 2D magnetism, which has seen rapid progress since 2016.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical results on 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: Covers ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and multiferroics.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving and opening new directions for applications.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: A review of radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, focusing on wave-matter interactions and particle manipulation.
motivation: To provide a unified perspective on how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles, with applications in trapping, sorting, and pulling.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks and experimental demonstrations of optical and acoustic radiation forces and torques.
result: It summarizes key mechanisms and applications, including trapping of atoms and nanoparticles, cell sorting, and pulling forces.
conclusion: The review highlights the rich physics and practical potential of radiation forces and torques across optics and acoustics.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from multiple studies.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new electronic states.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: Spin glasses are a paradigmatic model for complex systems, and understanding their dynamics is important for many fields.
method: The review synthesizes experimental results, theoretical developments, and large-scale numerical simulations.
result: It tracks progress in spin-glass dynamics and highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich area for future research, with implications for diverse physical systems.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on material candidates and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in candidate materials, discussing their magnetic and topological properties.
result: Highlights key candidate materials and their chiral edge modes, but does not present new results.
conclusion: The review serves as a resource for researchers in quantum spin liquids, but is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to neural network data, but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a central problem in neuroscience, and statistical physics offers powerful tools for analyzing such complex systems.
method: The paper reviews the use of maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to analyze simultaneous recordings from thousands of neurons.
result: These methods uncover reproducible collective behaviors in neural populations, demonstrating that abstract theoretical principles can achieve predictive power comparable to other areas of physics.
conclusion: Statistical mechanics provides a quantitative bridge between neural data and theory, revealing emergent properties of neural networks.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a fundamental photophysical process, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models used to describe internal conversion, including nonradiative decay mechanisms and computational approaches.
result: The review summarizes the current state of theoretical methods and identifies key challenges and opportunities for future research.
conclusion: The authors provide an outlook on how these theoretical models can be incorporated into studies relevant to photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering formation interactions and quantum features.
motivation: To survey quantum-mechanical properties of skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum mechanics, including quantum tunneling and entanglement.
result: Summarizes current understanding of quantum effects in skyrmions, such as quantum depinning and superposition states.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmionics is an emerging field with open questions and potential for future quantum technologies.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, including their possible mediation by exotic bosons and implications for dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to probe fundamental symmetries through spin-dependent interactions beyond the Standard Model.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models of spin-dependent exotic interactions mediated by hypothetical bosons and surveys experimental techniques used to search for such interactions.
result: The review summarizes the current status of experimental constraints on various spin-dependent exotic interactions and outlines future directions.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain an active area of research with potential connections to dark matter and dark energy, but no definitive evidence has been found yet.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review on implementing fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for quantum simulation.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries, enabling simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Reviews experimental and theoretical approaches for realizing synthetic quantum matter in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions using atomic, photonic, and electronic platforms.
result: Summarizes progress in engineering exotic geometries and discusses potential for simulating topological phases and gravitational models.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries is a promising avenue for quantum simulation, but the paper is a broad review without deep technical contributions to the user's specific research directions.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on how active units align their orientation with their velocity, leading to novel collective behaviors.
motivation: To understand and unify the phenomenon of self-alignment in active systems, which can produce unique single-particle and collective dynamics not captured by standard alignment models.
method: The paper reviews existing theoretical models and experimental systems of self-alignment, presenting a unified mathematical framework and categorizing different types of self-alignment.
result: Self-alignment enables behaviors such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, with potential applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental mechanism in active matter that reshapes motion emergence, and its study opens new avenues for designing active materials and understanding biological systems.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of using massive quantum systems to probe gravity, including tests of quantum gravity effects like decoherence and entanglement.
motivation: To understand the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, which is poorly understood, by using massive quantum systems as probes.
method: Review of theoretical proposals and experimental efforts to detect gravity-induced decoherence, collapse, and entanglement between massive particles.
result: Summarizes current state-of-the-art experiments and theoretical models for testing quantum gravity with massive quantum systems.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity effects, but further experimental and theoretical work is needed.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: A Python library for modular optical design is presented and demonstrated for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical systems in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions are not scalable due to conventional piecewise setup.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, an open-source Python library that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable modular, path-based optical layouts, and created 3D-printed baseplates for common subsystems.
result: The system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates on strontium trapped ions, demonstrating laser cooling and qubit state detection.
conclusion: This modular approach enables scalable optical systems for quantum computers and fosters open-source collaborative hardware design.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: The paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) and variable bosonic excitations; applied to a benchmark lithium wave function.
result: The wave function is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five numerically significant, demonstrating superselection rules in configuration space.
conclusion: The decomposition provides a compact characterization and aids in searching for robust entangled states.

title: Experimental Exclusion Of A Generalized Károlyházy Gravity-induced Decoherence Model
authors: Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola And Catalina Curceanu
abstract: We report new experimental constraints on the generalized version of the gravity-induced decoherence model originally proposed by Károlyházy. Using data collected by the VIP Collaboration at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory with a high-purity germanium detector, we derive an improved lower bound on the spatial correlation length characterizing metric fluctuations in the model. We obtain a bound m (95% C.L.), which exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the previous experimental limit. When combined with the theoretical upper bound m derived from macroscopic localization requirements, our result excludes the generalized Károlyházy model. The same conclusion applies to an associated non-Markovian formulation of the continuous spontaneous localization model. Our findings significantly tighten experimental constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios and demonstrate the sensitivity of underground low-background experiments to foundational modifications of quantum mechanics.
tldr: Experimental exclusion of a gravity-induced decoherence model using underground detector data.
motivation: To test whether gravity causes wavefunction collapse via decoherence, which is a foundational question in quantum mechanics.
method: Analysis of high-purity germanium detector data from the VIP Collaboration to constrain the spatial correlation length in the generalized Károlyházy model.
result: New lower bound on the correlation length exceeds previous limits by an order of magnitude, excluding the model when combined with theoretical upper bounds.
conclusion: The generalized Károlyházy gravity-induced decoherence model is ruled out, tightening constraints on gravity-related modifications of quantum mechanics.

title: A Maxwell Fish-eye Lens In A Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Jelte Duchêne, Elinor Kath, Floriane Arrouas, Hanyi Jang, Helmut Strobel, Markus K Oberthaler, Jay Mehta, Liam M Farrell, Wyatt Kirkby And Duncan H J O’dell
abstract: We experimentally realize an analogue of the optical Maxwell fish-eye lens (MFEL) using phononic excitations in a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC). A MFEL is characterized by a radially symmetric, spatially varying refractive index with the remarkable property that rays emitted from any point within the lens are perfectly focused at their antipodal points. While the implementation of such gradient-index lenses is challenging in conventional optical systems, BECs offer a highly tunable platform in which the spatially varying speed of sound of collective excitations—phonons, the acoustic analogues of photons—can be engineered and their dynamics observed in real time. Time-resolved measurements of phonon wavefronts reveal focusing behavior that shows good agreement with analytical theory and numerical simulations. This work provides both a geometric and physical framework for engineering effective refractive indices using ultracold atoms, and simulating wave propagation on effective spherical geometries.
tldr: This paper experimentally realizes an analogue of the Maxwell fish-eye lens using phononic excitations in a Bose-Einstein condensate, demonstrating focusing of sound waves.
motivation: To create a highly tunable platform for studying gradient-index lenses and wave propagation on effective spherical geometries, which is challenging in conventional optics.
method: The authors engineer a spatially varying speed of sound in a BEC to mimic the refractive index profile of a Maxwell fish-eye lens, and observe phonon wavefront dynamics via time-resolved measurements.
result: Time-resolved measurements show focusing behavior that agrees well with analytical theory and numerical simulations.
conclusion: BECs provide a versatile analog system for simulating wave propagation in curved geometries and gradient-index optics, with potential applications in quantum simulation.

title: Quantum Phases And Stability Of Bose–Hubbard Triangular Ladder With Magnetic Field
authors: Yue Jian, Jun-Hua Luo, Zi-Fa Yu, Juan Zhang, Ying-Ge Xu And Ju-Kui Xue
abstract: We investigate the ground state properties of interacting bosons on a triangular ladder subject to an artificial magnetic field. By means of the mean-field approximation, rich phases are revealed in the limit of weak interaction and large bosons occupation per site, including the Meissner superfluid, vortex superfluid, biased chiral superfluid (C-SF), C-SF and insulating phases. The quantum phases can be precisely identified and the underlying physics of phase transitions can be clarified by utilizing order parameters based on the atomic density, the effective rung current, and the current asymmetry ratio. Meanwhile, the phase transition of the system can be effectively controlled by adjusting the rung-to-leg coupling ratio, the magnetic flux and the atomic interaction. Furthermore, using Bogoliubov theory, we have mapped the stability phase diagram across all parameters, and clarified the interdependence between superfluidity and the dispersion relation. The excitation spectrum, which effectively describes the system’s energetic stability, is governed by the rung-to-leg coupling ratio, the magnetic flux, and the atomic interaction. Numerical simulations validate the dynamical instability of the system. This work offers a theoretical foundation for identifying new quantum phases exhibited by ultracold atoms in optical lattices and new experimental approaches for achieving system superfluidity.
tldr: This paper studies ground state phases of bosons on a triangular ladder with a magnetic field using mean-field and Bogoliubov theory.
motivation: To understand quantum phases and stability of ultracold bosons in optical lattices under artificial magnetic fields.
method: Mean-field approximation and Bogoliubov theory are used to compute phase diagrams and excitation spectra.
result: Rich phases including Meissner superfluid, vortex superfluid, and chiral superfluids are identified; stability phase diagrams are mapped.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for identifying new quantum phases and controlling superfluidity in ultracold atom systems.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically simulate the propagation of vortex solitons.
result: They find two classes of stable vortex solitons with in-phase or out-of-phase bright spots, and show that low-charge vortex solitons can be stable, with stability intervals broadening as rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Quantum Algorithms For Viscosity Solutions To Nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi Equations Based On An Entropy Penalization Method
authors: Shi Jinnana Liuahttps://ror.org/0220qvk04institute Of Natural Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, Chinabhttps://ror.org/0220qvk04school Of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, Chinachttps://ror.org/0220qvk04ministry Of Education Key Laboratory In Scientific And Engineering Computing, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, Chinadhttps://ror.org/0220qvk04global College, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 24, June 2026.
SignificanceWe developed quantum algorithms for nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi equations that obviated several major obstacles for nonlinear partial differential equations:valid for general convex and strongly nonlinear Hamiltonian with small dissipation;valid ...
tldr: This paper presents quantum algorithms for solving nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi equations using an entropy penalization method.
motivation: Nonlinear partial differential equations are challenging for classical and quantum computers; the authors aim to develop quantum algorithms that overcome obstacles like nonlinearity and dissipation.
method: The approach uses an entropy penalization method to transform the nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi equation into a sequence of linear problems that can be solved on a quantum computer.
result: The quantum algorithms are shown to be valid for general convex and strongly nonlinear Hamiltonians with small dissipation, providing a polynomial speedup over classical methods.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a viable quantum approach for a class of nonlinear PDEs, but the connection to quantum information or thermodynamics is indirect.

title: Dual Enhancement Of Superconductivity In FeSe/SrTiO3 Via Orbital And Correlation Synergy
authors: Guihao Jiajingming Yanyucong Pengshendong Supei Ouyangxiaopeng Huqi-Kun Xuewei Liahttps://ror.org/03cve4549state Key Laboratory Of Low-Dimensional Quantum Physics, Department Of Physics, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, Chinabfrontier Science Center For Quantum Information, Beijing 100084, Chinachttps://ror.org/04nqf9k60beijing Academy Of Quantum Information Sciences, Beijing 100193, Chinadhttps://ror.org/049tv2d57southern University Of Science And Technology, Shenzhen 518055, Chinaehefei National Laboratory, Hefei 230088, China
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 24, June 2026.
SignificanceIn iron-based superconductors, thedz2orbital band lies deep below the Fermi energy and is conventionally excluded from the superconducting pairing process. This work overturns this view. Using a scanning tunneling microscope tip to apply ...
tldr: This paper reports a scanning tunneling microscope study of FeSe/SrTiO3, showing that tip-induced electric field can enhance superconductivity by involving the dz2 orbital and correlation effects.
motivation: To understand the role of the dz2 orbital in iron-based superconductors, which is usually considered irrelevant for pairing, and to explore new ways to enhance superconductivity.
method: Using a scanning tunneling microscope tip to apply an electric field and measure local density of states on FeSe/SrTiO3 thin films.
result: The electric field induces a Lifshitz transition that brings the dz2 band to the Fermi level, increasing the superconducting gap and critical temperature via orbital and correlation synergy.
conclusion: The dz2 orbital can actively participate in superconductivity, and electric-field control offers a new route to enhance Tc in iron-based superconductors.

title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Approach For Melt Pool Prediction In Laser Powder Bed Fusion
authors: Kincho H. Law Matthew M. Sato
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a promising additive manufacturing technique that suffers from quality assurance concerns. Predicting melt pools from process parameters is crucial for assessing quality prior to manufacturing but remains a difficult problem because of the complex physical processes underlying LPBF. Quantum computers present a new computing paradigm, providing a new approach to information processing using quantum entanglement and superposition. This paper presents a practical demonstration of a hybrid quantum-classical model that leverages quantum computing to improve process parameter feature extraction with a quantum feature encoder. To make the quantum approach computationally feasible for large datasets, we first employ a clustering algorithm to reduce the number of expensive quantum computations. These quantum features are then processed by a classical neural network to predict the melt pool morphology, allowing for more accurate predictions of melt pools. We demonstrate the method using a quantum simulator, analyze the effect of measurement shot noise on the predictive performance of the network, and verify the results using quantum hardware. Finally, by examining which quantum features are most important, we provide insights that can inform the future design of more effective quantum encoding circuits. Ultimately, the performance improvement over purely classical networks validates the hybrid approach, demonstrating an engineering application of quantum computing using noisy and intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical model uses quantum feature encoding and classical neural networks to predict melt pool morphology in laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.
motivation: Quality assurance in LPBF is challenging due to complex physics; predicting melt pools from process parameters is crucial but difficult.
method: A clustering algorithm reduces dataset size, then a quantum feature encoder extracts features processed by a classical neural network to predict melt pool morphology.
result: The hybrid approach outperforms purely classical networks on a quantum simulator and is verified on quantum hardware, with analysis of measurement shot noise and feature importance.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical NISQ-era application of quantum computing for engineering, validating hybrid quantum-classical models for additive manufacturing.

title: Forms, Half-densities, And The Quantum Odd Symplectic Category In The Bv Formalism
authors: Pavol \v{s}evera
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note is a detailed review of the geometry behind the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism and how it fits into the framework of the quantum odd symplectic category and the odd quantization functor.
tldr: A detailed review of the geometry behind the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism and its relation to the quantum odd symplectic category.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive geometric understanding of the BV formalism, which is used in quantization of gauge theories.
method: The paper reviews and synthesizes known geometric structures, including half-densities and odd symplectic categories.
result: It clarifies how the BV formalism fits into the framework of the quantum odd symplectic category and the odd quantization functor.
conclusion: The geometric perspective offers a unified view of the BV formalism, but the work is primarily a review without new results.

title: Dual-isotope Narrow-line Mot Of Dysprosium By Phase Modulation
authors: M. D\"urbeck, L. Reihs, J. Seifert, B. Choudhari, J. P. Marulanda-Serna, N. Werum, M. de Pas, G. Meijer, G. Valtolina
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on the characterization of a narrow-line magneto-optical trap (MOT), where two different isotopes of the dysprosium (Dy) atom can be simultaneously loaded and trapped. We rely on phase modulation via high-power, free-space electro-optic modulators (EOMs) to generate optical sidebands at the correct detuning for two different isotopes. This technique is applied on the slowing transition at 421 nm and the MOT transition at 626 nm. Using modular resonant electronic circuits, we match the sideband separation to the isotope shift among the two target isotopes, realizing mixtures of the bosonic isotopes 164Dy -162Dy and 162Dy -160Dy. We exploit the interplay between radiation forces and gravity in the narrow-line MOT to control the spatial position of the two isotopes with the EOM drive frequency. We demonstrate full control of the isotopic mixture with the EOM drive, offering new and cost-effective capabilities for controlling mixtures of atomic species that can be trapped in a narrow-line MOT.
tldr: This paper reports a narrow-line magneto-optical trap for two dysprosium isotopes using phase modulation, enabling control of isotopic mixtures.
motivation: To develop a cost-effective method for trapping and controlling mixtures of atomic isotopes, which is relevant for quantum simulation and precision measurements.
method: Phase modulation via free-space electro-optic modulators generates optical sidebands at the correct detuning for two isotopes; modular resonant circuits match sideband separation to isotope shifts.
result: Simultaneous trapping of 164Dy-162Dy and 162Dy-160Dy mixtures is achieved, with spatial control of isotopes via EOM drive frequency.
conclusion: The technique offers new capabilities for controlling atomic mixtures in narrow-line MOTs, but does not directly advance quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems as defined.

title: Hessian-augmented Supervised Learning For Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman PDEs
authors: Mat\'ias G\'omez-Aedo, Behzad Azmi, Yuyang Huang, Dante Kalise, Karl Kunisch
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A data-driven method is developed for approximating value functions in deterministic optimal control problems with nonlinear control-affine dynamics. The Pontryagin Maximum Principle optimality system is solved from multiple initial conditions to generate training data consisting of values, gradients, and Hessians of the value function, where Hessian information is obtained from a matrix Riccati equation along optimal trajectories. These quantities augment a weighted least-squares regression over sparse polynomial bases on hyperbolic cross index sets, with gradients and Hessians contributing additional linear equations per sample and substantially reducing sample complexity compared to value-only regression. Feedback laws are recovered analytically from the learned value function. In high dimensions, a partial Hessian strategy controls the cost of data generation. The approach is validated on problems of increasing state dimension, where second-order data augmentation is shown to improve approximation accuracy and closed-loop performance, with up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in the number of training samples required relative to lower-order methods.
tldr: A data-driven method using Hessian-augmented regression to solve Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman PDEs for optimal control.
motivation: To improve sample efficiency and accuracy in approximating value functions for high-dimensional optimal control problems.
method: Generates training data (values, gradients, Hessians) by solving Pontryagin's optimality system and Riccati equations, then performs weighted least-squares regression over sparse polynomial bases.
result: Second-order data augmentation reduces sample complexity by up to an order of magnitude compared to value-only or gradient-only methods.
conclusion: Hessian augmentation is an effective strategy for data-driven approximation of value functions in deterministic optimal control.

title: How Many Rf Chains Does A Microwave Linear Analog Computer (MiLAC) Need To Match The Fully-Digital Cram\'er-Rao Bound?
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Yu Ge, Bruno Clerckx, Tareq Y. Al-Naffouri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A microwave linear analog computer (MiLAC) is a tunable microwave network that performs linear operations directly on radio-frequency signals through wave propagation. Used as an antenna-array front end, it can map many antenna signals to a small number of active RF chains. While lossless reciprocal MiLACs have been shown to provide flexible or capacity-achieving beamforming for wireless communications, their sensing performance remains largely unexplored. We analyze direction-of-arrival estimation for [MATH] far-field targets using a tunable receive-side lossless reciprocal MiLAC combiner. We show that the Fisher information matrix depends on the combiner only through the orthogonal projector onto its row space and never exceeds that of a fully digital receiver. Equality holds when the row space contains the [MATH]-dimensional joint steering--derivative subspace, establishing a zero-gap threshold of two RF chains per target. A dimension-counting argument lower-bounds the number of tunable components required to achieve the digital Cram\'er--Rao bound for every target configuration. The stem-connected MiLAC attains this bound asymptotically, up to an antenna-count-independent additive overhead, while scaling linearly with the antenna and target counts. Unlike a phase-shifter front end with the same number of RF chains, MiLAC can exactly attain the fully digital bound. Numerical results validate the analysis.
tldr: This paper analyzes the number of RF chains needed for a microwave linear analog computer (MiLAC) to match the Cramér-Rao bound in direction-of-arrival estimation.
motivation: To understand the sensing performance of MiLAC as an antenna-array front end, which has been studied for communications but not for sensing.
method: The authors derive the Fisher information matrix for direction-of-arrival estimation using a lossless reciprocal MiLAC combiner and compare it to a fully digital receiver.
result: They show that the MiLAC can achieve the digital Cramér-Rao bound with two RF chains per target, and the stem-connected MiLAC attains this bound asymptotically.
conclusion: MiLAC can match the fully digital bound with a small number of RF chains, outperforming phase-shifter front ends.

title: Dynamical Low-rank Methods For The Wigner Equation I: Separable Difference Potential
authors: Yuehan Shao Sihong Shao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) have demonstrated its effectiveness in high-dimensional simulations. However, existing DLRA algorithms still face significant challenges when handling systems that involve complex collision terms, including the pseudo-differential operator ([MATH]) in the Wigner equation, a representative operator characterized by nonlocality. It is deserving to carry out a series of works to develop the DLRA algorithms for solving the Wigner equation. As the first step in this series of works, we propose an efficient DLRA algorithm for the Wigner equation, using a separable decomposition of the difference potential. We combine this separable assumption with two often-used truncations of [MATH], namely [MATH]-truncation and [MATH]-truncation, to obtain a kind of separated representation of [MATH]. Complexity analysis and several challenging experiments, including harmonic oscillators, Gaussian barrier scattering, electron-electron scattering, and a Helium-like system, all of which satisfy the separable assumption, confirm that the proposed DLRA algorithm has significant advantages, achieving a reduction in computational effort by one to two orders of magnitude in both runtime and memory requirements compared to the full-grid approach. It is worth noting that, even in the absence of a predetermined low-rank structure for the solution, DLRA can still serve as a numerical scheme that balances efficiency and accuracy.
tldr: This paper develops a dynamical low-rank approximation algorithm for solving the Wigner equation with a separable difference potential, achieving significant computational speedups.
motivation: High-dimensional simulations of quantum systems using the Wigner equation are computationally expensive due to the nonlocal pseudo-differential operator. Existing DLRA methods struggle with such complex collision terms.
method: The authors propose a DLRA algorithm that exploits a separable decomposition of the difference potential and combines it with two truncations of the pseudo-differential operator to obtain a separated representation.
result: The algorithm reduces runtime and memory requirements by one to two orders of magnitude compared to full-grid methods, as demonstrated on harmonic oscillators, Gaussian barrier scattering, electron-electron scattering, and a Helium-like system.
conclusion: The proposed DLRA algorithm is an efficient numerical scheme for the Wigner equation, balancing accuracy and computational cost, even when the solution lacks a predetermined low-rank structure.

title: Certified Reachable Sets For Nonlinear Reaction--Diffusion Systems
authors: Mohamed Amine Ouchdiri, Mohamed Maghenem, Saad Benjelloun, Adnane Saoud
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reachability analysis for dynamical systems seeks to compute a set containing all reachable states at a given time. Compared to ordinary differential equations (ODEs), the analysis of nonlinear reaction--diffusion PDEs with parametric uncertainties remains largely underexplored, due to the infinite-dimensional state space and the variety of solutions under different parameters. We address this through a three-step procedure: 1) Finite Element Methods (FEM)s to discretise the space and generate a finite-dimensional FEM-based model, 2) Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) to build a Reduced-Order Model (ROM), and 3) set-based reachability-analysis methods applied to the ROM. We propose a framework that enables us to derive explicit upper bounds on the approximation errors introduced at each stage of the pipeline. In particular, we quantify the discrepancy between trajectories of the original PDE and those of the FEM-based discretization, as well as the error between the FEM-based model and the reduced-order model. Importantly, these bounds are shown to hold uniformly over the considered set of parameters. By combining these error estimates, we obtain an over-approximation of the reachable set of the original PDE. The approach is illustrated on the Allen--Cahn equation and a logistic growth PDE.
tldr: A framework for certified reachable set computation of nonlinear reaction-diffusion PDEs using FEM, POD, and set-based reachability analysis.
motivation: Reachability analysis for nonlinear PDEs with parametric uncertainties is underexplored due to infinite-dimensional state spaces.
method: Discretize the PDE via FEM, reduce dimensionality via POD, then apply set-based reachability on the reduced-order model with explicit error bounds.
result: Explicit uniform error bounds between original PDE, FEM model, and ROM are derived, enabling over-approximation of the reachable set.
conclusion: The approach provides a certified over-approximation for nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, demonstrated on Allen-Cahn and logistic growth PDEs.

title: Cryptographic Certificates Of Validity For Trustworthy Ai
authors: Murdoch J. Gabbay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose cryptographic certificates of validity for agentic AI systems. The core idea is to formally specify a correctness or policy condition as a logical predicate, compile this predicate to a witness-checking problem over polynomial constraints, and use a succinct cryptographic proof system (and optionally zero-knowledge) to certify that the condition holds. This offers a middle ground between formal verification of source code, and cryptographic authentication. An agent's action can be accompanied by an independently checkable proof that it satisfies an agreed formal policy, without requiring the verifier to trust the agent or to re-execute computation. We outline the approach at a high level, give the core mathematical translation, relate the proposal to proof-carrying code, zkVMs, formal methods, and agent governance, and note the specification, auditing, and deployment questions that a full implementation must answer.
tldr: Proposes cryptographic certificates for AI systems using succinct proofs to verify policy compliance.
motivation: To bridge formal verification and cryptographic authentication for trustworthy AI agents.
method: Formalizes correctness conditions as logical predicates, compiles them to polynomial constraints, and uses succinct cryptographic proofs (e.g., zk-SNARKs) to certify compliance.
result: Outlines a high-level framework and mathematical translation, relating to proof-carrying code and zkVMs.
conclusion: The approach offers a middle ground but requires further specification, auditing, and deployment work.

title: Stability Checking Of Markov Jump Linear Systems Via Probabilistic Temporal Logic (Extended Version)
authors: Holger Hermanns Lena Becker
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Markov jump linear systems (MJLSs) model dynamical phenomena subject to random switching among multiple linear modes, driven by an underlying Markov chain. Classical notions such as mean and mean-square stability characterize the long-term asymptotic behaviour of the first and second moments of an MJLS, but they can be overly conservative or even misleading when only a specific subset of initial conditions is of interest. We tackle this challenge through the lens of model checking, where reasoning about specific sets of initial conditions is intrinsic to the approach. We begin by formalizing probabilistic computation tree logic (PCTL) on MJLSs, enabling the specification of state-based temporal properties for these systems. Building on this foundation, we extend the logic to capture moment-based stability properties relative to a prescribed set of initial states. While we ultimately do not obtain a decision procedure for the entire base logic, the logical extensions can be handled -- albeit with some technical subtleties -- by exploiting linear-algebraic techniques.
tldr: This paper studies stability checking of Markov jump linear systems using probabilistic temporal logic, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Classical stability notions for MJLSs can be overly conservative when only specific initial conditions are of interest; the authors aim to use model checking to reason about stability for prescribed initial states.
method: The paper formalizes probabilistic computation tree logic (PCTL) on MJLSs and extends it to capture moment-based stability properties, leveraging linear-algebraic techniques.
result: A decision procedure for the full base logic is not obtained, but the logical extensions can be handled using linear-algebraic methods.
conclusion: The approach provides a way to check stability for specific initial conditions, but the logic remains partially undecidable.

title: Cyclic Denoising Reveals Ultrastable Memories In Diffusion Models
authors: Stefano Martiniani Rishabh Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24000v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce cyclic denoising -- repeated forward and reverse diffusion at controlled noise amplitudes -- as an extraction attack for image diffusion models. Inspired by random organization in disordered solids, cyclic denoising exposes regions of the learned distribution that are largely inaccessible to standard sampling. The dynamics drive samples toward attractors with a broad stability spectrum. The deepest attractors are ultrastable: they regenerate after near-total corruption and persist through thousands of noising-denoising cycles. Many of these attractors correspond to memorized training images, including stock photographs, brand watermarks, and web-crawl artifacts. The attack requires only sampler-level control, with no gradients, weight inspection, prompts, captions, or prior knowledge of the training data. Unlike generate-and-filter attacks, which rely on large-scale prompted generation and post-hoc similarity or membership-inference filtering, our main protocol is fully unconditioned. We demonstrate the phenomenon in Stable Diffusion v1.4 and in a pixel-space DDPM, showing consistent behavior across latent- and pixel-space diffusion models. Across noise amplitudes, we observe a yielding-like transition: low-amplitude cycling produces trivial absorbing fixed points or limit cycles, while larger amplitudes induce rearrangements, basin hopping, and long-lived trapping in structured memorized attractor basins. We also observe hierarchical partial absorption, prompt-stabilized basins, and cross-initial-condition universality of the recovered attractor set. Our results therefore show that cyclic denoising is both a physics-inspired probe of generative landscapes and a practical tool for memorization auditing, with implications for privacy, copyright compliance, and model fingerprinting.
tldr: Cyclic denoising is introduced as an extraction attack on diffusion models, revealing ultrastable memorized images.
motivation: To probe the learned distribution of diffusion models and extract memorized training data without prior knowledge.
method: Repeated forward and reverse diffusion at controlled noise amplitudes (cyclic denoising) drives samples toward attractors.
result: Deep attractors correspond to memorized training images, surviving thousands of cycles; a yielding-like transition is observed.
conclusion: Cyclic denoising serves as both a physics-inspired probe and a practical tool for memorization auditing.

tldr: This paper studies the phase diagram of twisted bilayer cuprates, focusing on competing superconducting states and time-reversal symmetry breaking.
motivation: Experiments on twisted cuprate Josephson junctions show conflicting signatures of time-reversal symmetry breaking, and the authors aim to explain this variability.
method: The authors perform a microscopic theoretical exploration of the phase diagram as a function of twist angle, filling, and interlayer tunneling strength.
result: They find that distinct competing superconducting states are stabilized depending on microscopic parameters, clarifying the origin of device-dependent experimental outcomes.
conclusion: The variability in experimental signatures can be understood from microscopic parameters, but the work does not directly connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

motivation: To understand how electronic conductivity affects phonon behavior in rutile oxides, which is relevant to condensed matter physics.
method: Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy on metallic (RuO2, IrO2) and insulating (TiO2, GeO2) rutile oxides.
result: Metallic compounds exhibit anomalous phonon softening and broadening due to electron-phonon coupling, while insulators show conventional anharmonic behavior.
conclusion: Nonadiabatic phonon renormalization is significant in metallic rutiles, highlighting the role of electron-phonon interactions.

method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations for (001)- and (111)-oriented films under various strain conditions.
result: Strain and orientation significantly modify structural distortions and magnetic ordering, with potential for tuning multiferroic behavior.
conclusion: Epitaxial strain is an effective tool to control magnetic properties in this double perovskite, but no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

tldr: This paper studies ballistic aggregation in active matter systems of self-aligning adhesive particles, inspired by motile cells in tissue formation.
motivation: To understand the fast aggregation observed in adhesive active matter, such as motile cells, by identifying the underlying kinetic regime.

result: A flocking transition leads to ballistic aggregation where cluster persistence length grows faster with mass than intercluster distance.
conclusion: Collective ballistic motion explains the rapid aggregation in adhesive active matter, providing insight into tissue formation and similar processes.

method: The authors derive a hydrodynamic theory based on continuum equations for active particle density and orientation, incorporating activity and repulsive interactions.
result: The theory predicts wetting transitions and contact angles that depend on activity, with active particles showing enhanced wetting compared to passive systems.
conclusion: Active wetting is qualitatively different from passive wetting, and the hydrodynamic theory captures key features observed in simulations and experiments.

result: They characterize the dynamic critical behavior and determine critical exponents associated with the rigidity transition.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the dynamic aspects of rigidity percolation, but it is a classical statistical mechanics problem without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

result: The method achieves accurate long-term predictions with significant speedup compared to conventional MD simulations.

conclusion: The ghost mechanism provides a theoretical framework for abrupt learning in recurrent networks, with implications for training dynamics.

Author(s): Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, and Philipp Gegenwart

Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground states, reached via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021043] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in a kagome spin ice compound, revealing hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.
motivation: To investigate the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome ice compound HoAgGe, which may host exotic magnetic order.
method: Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements combined with neutron scattering and other techniques to probe the phase transition and symmetry breaking.
result: The system exhibits a three-dimensional XY universality class transition and hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground state.
conclusion: The study provides evidence for a novel magnetic ground state in kagome ice systems, relevant to frustrated magnetism.

title: Robust Orbital-Selective Flat Bands In Layered Transition-Metal Oxyhalides At Room Temperature
authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin

Author(s): Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, and Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021041] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature using ARPES.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum states, but many are only stable at low temperatures; this work aims to find room-temperature flat bands.
method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was used to measure the electronic band structure of layered transition-metal oxyhalides.
result: Intrinsic flat bands that are orbital-selective and remain stable at room temperature were observed.
conclusion: These materials provide a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states at accessible temperatures.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
