Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding anisotropy in silica films can inform better coating design.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to reveal hidden anisotropy.
result: They find that silica films exhibit anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, affecting mechanical properties.
conclusion: The discovery guides coating deposition and postprocessing strategies to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Intertwined Polar, Chiral, And Ferro-Rotational Orders In A Homo-Ferro-Rotational Insulator
authors: Weizhe Zhang, June Ho Yeo, Xiaoyu Guo, Tony Chiang, Nishkarsh Agarwal, John T. Heron, Kai Sun, Junjie Yang, Sang-Wook Cheong, Youngjun Ahn, And Liuyan Zhao
abstract:
Author(s): Weizhe Zhang, June Ho Yeo, Xiaoyu Guo, Tony Chiang, Nishkarsh Agarwal, John T. Heron, Kai Sun, Junjie Yang, Sang-Wook Cheong, Youngjun Ahn, and Liuyan Zhao

Multimodal optical characterization of Ni
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021030] Published Fri May 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of intertwined polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational orders in a homo-ferro-rotational insulator using multimodal optical characterization.
motivation: To understand the coupling between different ferroic orders and the formation of complex domain walls in a material with a uniform ferro-rotational state.
method: Multimodal optical characterization techniques were used to study the material Ni2MnSe4.
result: The study identifies a uniform ferro-rotational state that couples polarity and chirality, leading to complex mixed-type domain walls.
conclusion: The findings reveal a new type of multiferroic order with intertwined polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational degrees of freedom.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper reviews the theoretical background of Wannier functions and describes the interoperable software ecosystem, including codes for maximally localized Wannier functions and their applications.
result: It highlights the widespread use of Wannier functions in computing topological invariants, Berry phases, and other material properties.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling accurate and insightful materials simulations.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies uniaxial-stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on the coupling between magnetic order and elastic properties.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic phases in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice shrinkage and dramatic stiffening of the lattice, indicating magnetic order 'locking'.
conclusion: The strong magnetoelastic coupling suggests that similar effects may occur in other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for analyzing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills, and uncovers a hidden symmetry.
motivation: To understand non-planar corrections in AdS/CFT by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: All four-point functions with two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons are computed, revealing a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression.
motivation: To understand the microscopic electrostatic landscape in graphene devices with metal-oxide layers, which is crucial for device engineering but typically inferred indirectly.
method: In operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution is used to image the valence band edge across the device under bias and gate voltage.
result: The electric field in graphene covered with oxides is suppressed by up to 50%, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to uncover potential landscapes in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.

title: Weyl Orbit Particles
authors: Martin T. Luu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mass spectrum of affine Toda theory is known to be expressible in terms of a suitable eigenvector of the relevant Cartan matrix. The particles correspond in a precise manner to the Coxeter element orbits in the set of roots. Recently, variants of affine Toda theory have been constructed for many different Weyl group elements. Again, the particles correspond to orbits in the set of roots and this allows the calculation of the classical mass spectrum. We show how these spectral calculations generalize the affine Toda relation with the Cartan matrix. As an example, we calculate the spectrum for the unique non-Coxeter infinite family [MATH] of primitive regular conjugacy classes in the Weyl groups of complex simple Lie algebras.
tldr: This paper studies the mass spectrum of affine Toda theory and its generalizations using Weyl group orbits, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand the mass spectrum of affine Toda theories and their variants in terms of Weyl group orbits.
method: The paper generalizes the relation between affine Toda mass spectra and Cartan eigenvectors to other Weyl group elements, using root system orbits.
result: It shows how spectral calculations generalize the affine Toda relation and computes the spectrum for a non-Coxeter infinite family of primitive regular conjugacy classes.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical framework for mass spectra in Toda theories but does not address any of the user's research directions.

title: Scalable Reflective Communication For Microscopic Electronics
authors: Matthew F. Campbell, Kyle Skelil, Chaitanya Karimanasseri, David Gonzalez-Medrano, Li Xu, Jungho Lee, David T. Blaauw, Igor Bargatin, And Marc Z. Miskin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Untethered microscopic electronic circuits hold the potential for extraordinary advances in many fields such as neural transmitting and distributed sensing. However, establishing uplink communications from the microscale back to the macroscopic world remains challenging; existing micro-transmitters are difficult to integrate with semiconductor processing. Here we surmount this obstacle, introducing a strategy for modulating backscattered photons based on the electrochromic polymer PEDOT:PSS (poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate) that is scalable to micron-order sizes and manufacturable using standard parallelizable methods. Our devices, which we call SPOTs (submillimeter polymer optical transmitters), actuate at low voltages (< +/-1 V), switch in as fast as 10 {\mu}s, can run for millions of cycles, and operate seamlessly in electrolytes. We achieve this design by emphasizing architectural simplicity and mass-manufacturability rather than traditional metrics such as data rates or energy costs. As a demonstration, we develop SPOT-equipped temperature-sensitive photovoltaic-powered foundry-fabricated microchips and use them to wirelessly measure and transmit local temperatures. These results represent an important step toward fully-integrable, micron-scale bidirectional communication.
tldr: This paper presents a scalable method for microscopic electronic communication using electrochromic polymer modulators, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Untethered microscopic electronic circuits need uplink communication, but existing micro-transmitters are difficult to integrate with semiconductor processing.
method: The authors use the electrochromic polymer PEDOT:PSS to modulate backscattered photons, creating submillimeter polymer optical transmitters (SPOTs) that operate at low voltages and are manufacturable with standard methods.
result: SPOTs actuate at <±1 V, switch in 10 μs, run for millions of cycles, and work in electrolytes. They demonstrate temperature sensing and wireless transmission using photovoltaic-powered microchips.
conclusion: This work represents a step toward fully integrable, micron-scale bidirectional communication for microscopic electronics.

title: A Novel Arm-Length Stabilization Scheme For Gravitational-Wave Detectors With AlGaAs/GaAs Coated Mirrors
authors: Jian Liu, Juntao Pan, Carl Blair, Chiara Di Fronzo, Li Ju, Chunnong Zhao, Sheon S. Y. Chua, Bram J. J. Slagmolen, Nutsinee Kijbunchoo, David Ottaway
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The arm length stabilisation system is employed in gravitational-wave detectors to reduce the velocity of the mirrors such that the arm cavities can be brought onto resonance in a controlled manner required to attain the detector operating point. For future upgrades of current gravitational wave detectors such as A#, which will incorporate AlGaAs/GaAs coatings, the current frequency-doubled arm length stabilisation system is unsuitable due to excessive absorption of the frequency-doubled 532nm beam by the AlGaAs/GaAs coating. We propose a novel multi-wavelength arm length stabilisation scheme that uses both frequency-doubled and frequency-tripled beams. The 1596nm auxiliary locking beam is outside the absorption bands of AlGaAs/GaAs coating. It is frequencytripled to 532nm and phase-locked with the 1064nm science laser through its second harmonic at 532 nm. In a tabletop setup, we experimentally demonstrated the stable cavity detuning and robust cavity locking transition by controlling the 1596nm laser and 1064nm laser phase locked loop. This demonstration confirmed that the proposed novel arm length stabilisation scheme is compatible with future upgrades or third-generation gravitational wave detectors that use AlGaAs/GaAs-coated test masses.
tldr: This paper proposes a novel multi-wavelength arm-length stabilization scheme for gravitational-wave detectors using AlGaAs/GaAs coated mirrors.
motivation: Current frequency-doubled stabilization systems are unsuitable for future gravitational-wave detectors with AlGaAs/GaAs coatings due to excessive absorption of the 532nm beam.
method: The scheme uses a 1596nm auxiliary locking beam (outside absorption bands) frequency-tripled to 532nm and phase-locked with the 1064nm science laser via its second harmonic. A tabletop experiment demonstrated stable cavity detuning and robust locking transition.
result: The proposed scheme was experimentally validated, showing compatibility with future upgrades or third-generation gravitational-wave detectors using AlGaAs/GaAs-coated test masses.
conclusion: The multi-wavelength approach effectively overcomes absorption issues and provides a viable stabilization method for advanced gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Ground-State Energy Solutions Of The Lithium Atom: Zeroth-, First-, And Second-Order Perturbation Theory And The Variational Method
authors: Afraa Mahboubi, B\"u\c{s}ra G\"ok\c{c}e Zolmaz, Devrim Karayer, Handenur \c{s}ay, O\u{g}uzhan Kaya, Abdulkadir Senol
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, the ground-state energy of the lithium atom is systematically investigated using both time-independent perturbation theory and the variational method to provide a comprehensive pedagogical analysis of many-body atomic systems. The unperturbed Hamiltonian is initially constructed by neglecting electron-electron interactions, treating the system as three independent hydrogen-like electrons to yield a zeroth-order energy baseline of -275.51 eV. The antisymmetric fermionic nature of the exact wave function is rigorously enforced through the Slater determinant formalism. First-order perturbation theory is applied to evaluate static inter-electronic repulsion using exact Coulomb and exchange integrals, refining the energy state to -192.01 eV. To account for dynamical electronic correlation, second-order perturbation theory is computed numerically for virtual single-electron s-orbital transitions, leading to a total perturbative energy of -196.36 eV. A brief discussion of two-electron excitations is also included to encapsulate further physical realism within the framework. Furthermore, a non-orthogonal two-parameter variational approach is employed to model the shell-specific shielding effect. By optimizing the effective nuclear charges, the variational method establishes a superior upper bound energy of -201.187 eV. The results of both methods are comprehensively contrasted against each other and the reference baseline to provide critical insights into the nature of electron correlation and screening in multi-electron atoms.
tldr: This paper computes the ground-state energy of the lithium atom using perturbation theory and variational methods, serving as a pedagogical exercise in atomic physics.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive pedagogical analysis of many-body atomic systems by systematically applying perturbation theory and variational methods to the lithium atom.
method: Time-independent perturbation theory (zeroth, first, second order) with Slater determinant wavefunctions, and a non-orthogonal two-parameter variational approach optimizing effective nuclear charges.
result: Zeroth-order energy -275.51 eV, first-order -192.01 eV, second-order -196.36 eV, variational upper bound -201.187 eV.
conclusion: The variational method provides a superior upper bound compared to perturbation theory, highlighting the importance of electron correlation and screening in multi-electron atoms.

title: Precise One-dimensional Nanochannels In Transition Metal Dichalcogenides As Building Blocks For Advanced Nanophotonics
authors: Abhay V. Agrawal, Wouter Holman, Bet\"ul K\"u\c{c}\"uk\"oz, Tomasz J. Antosiewicz, Timur O. Shegai
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomically sharp edges are essential for future high-index nanophotonic structures, yet conventional lithography and dry etching methods inevitably introduce edge roughness that limits optical confinement and reproducibility. Recently, anisotropic wet etching of multilayer van der Waals crystals, such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), has enabled crystallographically defined, atomically sharp zigzag edges, eliminating the edge-roughness problem. However, the process is intrinsically limited to confined geometries such as isolated triangular or hexagonal features dictated by crystal stacking symmetry. Here, we demonstrate a lithography-guided anisotropic etching framework that drives TMDs etching beyond isolated confined geometries by enforcing controlled interaction of neighboring etched nanoholes regions. In multilayer 2H-WS2, merging of anisotropic etch fronts enables sustained long-range propagation of zigzag facets, introducing a previously inaccessible 180-degree edge alignment and a crystallographically defined design space combining 120-degree and 180-degree junctions. Using this approach, we fabricate extended nanophotonic structures with ultrasharp sidewalls, including sub-100-nm-gap one-dimensional gratings, waveguides, defect-engineered photonic cavities, angle programmed photonic lattices, and diffractive zone plates. Back-focal-plane reflection spectroscopy of atomically sharp 1D periodic 2H-WS2 gratings demonstrates their photonic functionality, revealing symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum (SP-BICs) and strong exciton-photon coupling in multilayer WS2. Finally, we fabricate ultrathin, ultranarrow, and ultralong nanoribbons with record-high aspect ratios. Together, these results demonstrate edge merging as a generic route to fabricate edge-defined, atomically sharp nanophotonic and nanoelectronic architectures in layered van der Waals platforms.
tldr: This paper presents a lithography-guided anisotropic etching method to fabricate atomically sharp nanophotonic structures in transition metal dichalcogenides, demonstrating extended gratings, waveguides, and cavities with bound states in the continuum.
motivation: Conventional lithography introduces edge roughness that limits optical confinement; the authors aim to create atomically sharp edges for high-index nanophotonic devices.
method: They combine lithography with anisotropic wet etching of multilayer 2H-WS2 to merge etch fronts, enabling long-range propagation of zigzag facets and fabrication of sub-100-nm-gap gratings, waveguides, and photonic cavities.
result: They achieve symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum and strong exciton-photon coupling in multilayer WS2, and fabricate nanoribbons with record-high aspect ratios.
conclusion: Edge merging provides a generic route to fabricate atomically sharp nanophotonic and nanoelectronic architectures in layered van der Waals materials.

title: Enhancing Speckle Metrology With Diffusion Denoising In Photon-Starved Regimes
authors: Admir Bajraktarevic, Alexander C. Trowbridge, Saba N. Khan, Anton van Den Hengel, Graham D. Bruce, Kishan Dholakia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laser speckle is a powerful tool for precision metrology that enables highly sensitive measurements of light sources and subtle environmental perturbations. Many applications require operation in photon-limited regimes, for example when using low-power illumination or in spectral regions where sensitive detectors are unavailable. In these conditions, the structured speckle pattern that encodes the signal becomes challenging to disentangle from measurement noise, severely degrading performance. Here, we introduce a denoising framework to separate measurement noise from the underlying speckle structure in low-signal data. Using a hybrid pre-training and experimental fine-tuning strategy, the model is adapted using a small experimental dataset and integrates directly with existing speckle metrology pipelines. Applied to femtometre-scale wavelength sensing using an integrating sphere, the approach reduces root-mean-square error in low-signal conditions by up to 72% and enables accurate reconstruction where conventional speckle metrology fails.
tldr: This paper applies a diffusion denoising framework to improve speckle metrology in photon-starved regimes, achieving significant error reduction.
motivation: Speckle metrology suffers in low-light conditions due to noise obscuring the signal; existing methods fail to recover accurate measurements.
method: A hybrid pre-training and experimental fine-tuning strategy using a diffusion denoising model is developed to separate noise from speckle patterns.
result: The method reduces root-mean-square error by up to 72% in low-signal conditions and enables accurate reconstruction where conventional methods fail.
conclusion: The denoising framework effectively enhances speckle metrology in photon-limited regimes, with potential applications in precision sensing.

title: Traveling Profiles And Control Cost For A Pde Describing The Evolution Of Invasive Species
authors: Chiara Trifone Stefano Bianchini
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a detailed analysis of optimal traveling waves [MATH] for a model of invasive-species control proposed in [Bressan, Chiri, and Salehi, Math. Models Methods Appl. Sci., 2022] : the relative density [MATH] of the invasive species satisfies the following reaction-diffusion equation with a positive control U_t = U_{xx} + f(U) - \tilde \alpha(t,x) U, \quad U \in [0,1], \ \tilde \alpha \geq 0. The control [MATH] represents the fraction of the population removed at [MATH]: the minimal control effort [MATH] required to sustain a traveling invasion front with prescribed speed [MATH] is defined as the minimal [MATH]-norm of [MATH] for a traveling wave solution [MATH] to the PDE. In order to study large scale dynamics [MATH], a fundamental role is played by the structure of traveling waves and the convexity and regularity properties of [MATH]. The main results of this paper are the following: 1)In the phase plane [MATH], there exists a unique optimal profile [MATH] minimizing the effort; 2) It satisfies explicit first-order conditions, which are both necessary and sufficient; 3) The associated control is acting on an open subset of the set [MATH], in particular it is uniformly integrable, and it depends smoothly on [MATH] on a dense open set; 4)The effort function [MATH] is only [MATH] w.r.t. [MATH] and Lipschitz w.r.t. [MATH] in the [MATH]-topology, and is asymptocally linear for [MATH]; 5)[MATH] is in general neither convex nor subadditive.
tldr: This paper analyzes optimal traveling waves and control cost for a PDE model of invasive species control.
motivation: To understand the minimal control effort required to sustain a traveling invasion front with prescribed speed in a reaction-diffusion model.
method: Phase plane analysis and optimal control theory are used to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the optimal profile and control.
result: Existence and uniqueness of the optimal profile, explicit first-order conditions, and regularity properties of the effort function are established.
conclusion: The effort function is not convex nor subadditive, and the control is uniformly integrable and smooth on a dense open set.

title: Diagonal Frog: High-order Positivity-preserving Fd Schemes For Anisotropic Fokker-Planck Equations
authors: Andrey Itkin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Fokker-Planck equation is fundamental to statistical mechanics, yet in settings with multiple state variables, anisotropic (cross-) diffusion, and jumps, conventional discretizations frequently produce non-physical negative probability densities. Building on the operator approach of "A. Itkin, Pricing derivatives under Levy models. Modern finite difference and pseudo-differential operators approach, Springer, 2017, ISBN 978-1-4939-6792-6", we introduce a family of "Diagonal Frog" discretizations whose spatial operators are eventually M-matrices (EM-matrices). Although these operators lack a local M-matrix structure, positivity of the directional sub-operators emerges in the spirit of Zeno's paradox: the matrix exponential, assembled as the limit of infinitely many ever-smaller substeps, is provably nonnegative after a short transient even though no single substep is. For the mixed-derivative block, whose generator is not eventually nonnegative, positivity instead rests on a factorized resolvent solver and holds conditionally, on an explicit step-size window; discrete mass is conserved exactly by the splitting for every step size. The resulting schemes are second-order accurate in time and space and require O(m 2 N + m 3) operations per time step, where m is the dimension of the Krylov subspace used to apply the exponential. As stress tests, we solve a two-dimensional anisotropic Fokker-Planck equation in the strong cross-diffusion regime against an exact Gaussian reference, a Kramers escape problem in a double-well potential, and an advection-dominated problem, and observe that the schemes remain stable, nonnegative, and mass-conservative for a wide range of P\'ecklet numbers (so, don't need any flux limiter). Finally, we extend the construction to multidimensional processes and to the backward Kolmogorov equation with jumps.
tldr: This paper develops high-order positivity-preserving finite difference schemes for anisotropic Fokker-Planck equations using operator splitting and matrix exponentials.
motivation: Standard discretizations of Fokker-Planck equations with cross-diffusion often produce negative probability densities, which is unphysical. The author aims to construct schemes that guarantee nonnegative solutions while maintaining accuracy and efficiency.
method: The 'Diagonal Frog' family of discretizations uses spatial operators that are eventually M-matrices, combined with a factorized resolvent solver for mixed-derivative blocks. The matrix exponential is approximated via Krylov subspace methods, and the scheme is second-order accurate in time and space.
result: The schemes are proven to be positivity-preserving after a short transient and conditionally for mixed derivatives, with exact mass conservation. Numerical tests on 2D anisotropic Fokker-Planck, Kramers escape, and advection-dominated problems show stability, nonnegativity, and mass conservation for a wide range of Péclet numbers.
conclusion: The proposed Diagonal Frog schemes provide a robust numerical method for solving Fokker-Planck equations with anisotropic diffusion, ensuring physical positivity and mass conservation without flux limiters.

title: (Generalized) Spine Subalgebras Of Fourier-Stieltjes Algebras And Their Homomorphisms
authors: Nico Spronk, Ross Stokke, Aasaimani Thamizhazhagan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For any upper semilattice [MATH] of locally precompact topologies on a locally compact group [MATH], we define an associated generalized spine subalgebra [MATH] of the Fourier-Stieltjes algebra [MATH]. We show that [MATH] is a semilattice-graded [MATH]-direct sum of maximal copies of Fourier algebras and we identify its spectrum as a semilattice of groups. We build a collection of examples of generalized spine algebras over whose spectra we exhibit fine control. We define notions of compatible fusions of homomorphisms and affine maps, and use these definitions to characterize all completely positive, completely contractive and, when [MATH] is amenable, all completely bounded homomorphisms from a generalized spine algebra [MATH] to a Fourier-Stieltjes algebra [MATH]. These results are new, even when [MATH] is the full spine algebra [MATH] and even when [MATH] and [MATH] are abelian. We provide examples illustrating the scope of our theorems.
tldr: This paper studies generalized spine subalgebras of Fourier-Stieltjes algebras on locally compact groups and their homomorphisms.
motivation: To understand the structure and homomorphisms of certain subalgebras of Fourier-Stieltjes algebras, which are objects in abstract harmonic analysis.
method: The authors define generalized spine subalgebras using semilattices of topologies, show they are semilattice-graded direct sums, and characterize completely positive, completely contractive, and completely bounded homomorphisms.
result: They identify the spectrum as a semilattice of groups and provide a characterization of homomorphisms in terms of compatible fusions and affine maps.
conclusion: The results are new even for the full spine algebra and for abelian groups, extending the theory of Fourier-Stieltjes algebras.

title: Tractability Versus Curse Of Dimensionality For Geometric $L_p$-discrepancies
authors: Friedrich Pillichshammer Erich Novak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies tractability versus the curse of dimensionality for several geometric [MATH]-discrepancies through a unified discrepancy--integration duality framework, where worst case integration errors in suitable function spaces equal the corresponding discrepancies. A general lower bound method for non-negative linear rules in spaces under broad tensor-product assumptions establishes exponential information complexity in the dimension [MATH], yielding the curse of dimensionality for the respective discrepancy. We complement this overview by new results on discrepancy--integration duality and the curse of dimensionality for the periodic [MATH]-discrepancy. The current state of research on this general problem is summarized in a clearly laid out table, which also highlights the remaining open questions.
tldr: This paper studies the curse of dimensionality for geometric Lp-discrepancies using a discrepancy–integration duality framework.
motivation: Understanding whether high-dimensional numerical integration suffers from the curse of dimensionality is a fundamental question in approximation theory.
method: The authors develop a general lower bound method for non-negative linear rules under tensor-product assumptions and apply it to various Lp-discrepancies.
result: They prove exponential information complexity in the dimension for several discrepancies, establishing the curse of dimensionality, and provide new results for the periodic Lp-discrepancy.
conclusion: The paper summarizes the state of research on tractability of geometric discrepancies and highlights open questions.

title: Randomized Estimation Of T-Eigenvalues Of T-spd Tensors: A Two-Sided Bracket
authors: Nachiketa Mishra Hemant Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In earlier work we developed deterministic analytical bounds on the T-eigenvalues of symmetric positive definite (SPD) third-order tensors under the Kilmer--Martin T-product: the trace--determinant (TDet) bounds via the AM--GM inequality, and the trace-dependent (TDep) bounds generalizing Samuelson's inequality. While these bounds are cheap and guaranteed-valid, their relative gap grows as [MATH] in the tensor dimension [MATH], limiting their usefulness for large tensors. This paper develops randomized estimators for the extreme T-eigenvalues of T-SPD tensors that complement the deterministic bounds. We adapt the Halko--Martinsson--Tropp framework to the T-product setting and introduce four methods: (i) a randomized power method that produces a lower bound on [MATH] with exponential convergence; (ii) a randomized subspace iteration with a tensor-analogue HMT error bound; (iii) a two-sided rigorous bracket combining the randomized lower bound with the deterministic TDep upper bound; and (iv) a Hutchinson-based fully randomized TDep bound for matvec-only settings.
tldr: This paper develops randomized estimators for extreme T-eigenvalues of third-order tensors under the T-product, extending linear algebra techniques to tensor settings.
motivation: Deterministic bounds on T-eigenvalues become loose for large tensors, so randomized methods are needed to provide tighter estimates.
method: Adapts the Halko-Martinsson-Tropp randomized SVD framework to the T-product algebra, introducing a randomized power method, subspace iteration, two-sided bracket, and Hutchinson-based bound.
result: The randomized methods yield lower bounds with exponential convergence and complement deterministic upper bounds, producing rigorous intervals for extreme T-eigenvalues.
conclusion: Randomized estimators offer a practical way to bound T-eigenvalues for large T-SPD tensors where deterministic bounds are too weak.

title: Analysis And Approximation Of A Two-dimensional Induction Heating Problem
authors: Gabriel R. Barrenechea, Katherine Mackenzie, Abner Salgado
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we analyse the existence of solutions and finite element approximation of a steady-state two-dimensional induction heating problem. One of the main difficulties of the problem is its right-hand side which, at a first sight, is only integrable. Using a priori regularity results for the PDEs involved it is shown that the natural weak formulation of the problem can be justified. Then, we study the finite element approximation and prove that the standard Galerkin FEM converges in convex domains and under suitable conditions on the mesh. We improve on this result by applying the recently-proposed bound-preserving method (BPM) to the heat equation, and show that this method converges to a solution of the problem under less stringent conditions on the domain and the mesh. As these analyses are carried out without any assumption on regularity of the solutions, then the convergence of the finite element method also proves existence of solutions. Several numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results, and showcase the improvement provided by the use of the bound-preserving method over the standard finite element method.
tldr: This paper analyzes the existence of solutions and finite element approximation of a steady-state two-dimensional induction heating problem.
motivation: Induction heating is an important industrial process, but its mathematical analysis is challenging due to a right-hand side that is only integrable at first sight.
method: The authors use a priori regularity results for the PDEs to justify the weak formulation, then study standard Galerkin FEM and a bound-preserving method (BPM) for convergence.
result: They prove convergence of the standard FEM under convex domains and suitable mesh conditions, and show that BPM converges under less stringent conditions without regularity assumptions.
conclusion: The finite element method converges to a solution, and the bound-preserving method improves convergence conditions; numerical experiments confirm the theory.

title: Spectrally $n$-centered Operators. I
authors: Piotr Budzy\'nski
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the concept of spectrally [MATH]-centered operators and study it within the framework of unbounded weighted composition operators in [MATH]-spaces. Based on this, we establish a characterisation of spectrally centered unbounded weighted composition operators, generalising Giselsson's criterion to the unbounded regime. Finally, we analyse various associated conditions, highlighting the delicate measure-theoretic anomalies.
tldr: Introduces spectrally n-centered operators and characterizes them for unbounded weighted composition operators on L^p-spaces.
motivation: To generalize the concept of centered operators to the spectral setting and extend Giselsson's criterion to unbounded operators.
method: Develops the theory of spectrally n-centered operators and applies it to unbounded weighted composition operators using measure-theoretic analysis.
result: Provides a characterization of spectrally centered unbounded weighted composition operators, highlighting measure-theoretic anomalies.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for spectrally centered operators in the unbounded regime, with implications for operator theory.

abstract: ArXiv:2606.24608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In finite dimensions, every doubly stochastic matrix has the [MATH]-operator norm equal to [MATH] for all [MATH]. title: Rationalizing Collective Revealed Preferences With An Application In Fair Resource Allocation
authors: Chuwen Zhang, Zhiyun Guo, Zizhuo Wang, Yinyu Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a revealed preference approach for rationalizing collective consumption behavior. We introduce the Constructive Rationalization Method (CRM), which approximates the real market via a surrogate market of artificial consumers, called androids, with easy-to-compute demand functions. CRM uses observed aggregate demand and adds artificial consumers on the fly, while redistributing wealth under an empirical risk minimization principle. Unlike classical revealed preference approaches, CRM provides guarantees on the generalization risk for learning the aggregate demand function, while respecting the privacy of the underlying consumers in the real market. As an application, CRM can be used to provide reliable predictions for collective consumption behavior. Specifically, we show how to apply CRM to approximate allocations that are proportionally fair without requiring the knowledge of individual utilities.
tldr: This paper presents a revealed preference approach for rationalizing collective consumption behavior using artificial consumers, with an application to fair resource allocation.
motivation: Classical revealed preference approaches lack guarantees on generalization risk and privacy. The authors aim to provide a method that learns aggregate demand functions while preserving individual privacy.
method: The Constructive Rationalization Method (CRM) approximates the real market by introducing artificial consumers (androids) with easy-to-compute demand functions, using empirical risk minimization to redistribute wealth.
result: CRM provides guarantees on generalization risk for learning aggregate demand and can approximate proportionally fair allocations without knowledge of individual utilities.
conclusion: CRM offers a privacy-preserving, data-driven approach to rationalize collective consumption and predict fair resource allocations.

title: Token Complexity Of Certifying Stochastic-Oracle Reliability
authors: Jie Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wang~ introduced the Stochastic-Oracle Turing Machine (SOTM) framework and defined token complexity as the minimum expected cost of interacting with a stochastic oracle needed to attain a specified solution quality for a task. This paper develops an analogous notion for certifying the reliability of a stochastic oracle on a given domain. Certification token complexity is the minimum expected token cost required, with controlled error probability, to distinguish oracles that meet a target reliability level from those that fall below a lower reliability threshold. We construct an SPRT-based certification SOTM that queries the oracle, computes binary correctness scores, and stops when the accumulated log-likelihood evidence crosses a decision threshold. The SOTM halts almost surely, satisfies the desired two-sided error guarantee over the reliability regions to be certified, and yields an explicit upper bound on certification token complexity in terms of the reliability thresholds, the error bound, and the expected per-turn token cost. We then establish a matching information-theoretic lower bound: even with adaptive queries, every error-bounded certification SOTM must incur the same leading-order expected token cost as the SPRT-based construction as the prescribed error bound tends to zero. Together, these bounds characterize the leading-order certification token complexity in the small-error regime.
tldr: This paper introduces a token complexity framework for certifying the reliability of stochastic oracles using SPRT-based Turing machines.
motivation: To develop a rigorous measure of the expected cost (token complexity) required to certify whether a stochastic oracle meets a reliability threshold, with controlled error probability.
method: Constructs an SPRT-based certification Stochastic-Oracle Turing Machine (SOTM) that queries the oracle and stops when accumulated log-likelihood evidence crosses a decision threshold, and derives matching information-theoretic lower bounds.
result: Provides explicit upper and lower bounds on certification token complexity in the small-error regime, showing the SPRT-based construction is asymptotically optimal.
conclusion: The leading-order certification token complexity is characterized by the reliability thresholds, error bound, and expected per-turn token cost, with the SPRT-based SOTM achieving optimal performance.

title: Exact Schur-Sylvester Dimensionality Reductions For Non-Smooth Stochastic Complexity And Manifold Sampling
authors: Gary P. T. Choi Trenton Lau
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23867v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The exact computation of the Normalized Maximum Likelihood (NML) codelength for regular non-smooth estimators (e.g., Lasso) has been historically limited by the cubic scaling walls of manifold-constrained projection and volume integration. At each step of the geometric Propose-and-Project Metropolis--Hastings (PPMH) sampler, evaluating the projection operator requires inverting an [MATH] generalized KKT matrix, while calculating the volume factor requires the determinant of an [MATH] Gram matrix. This paper presents an exact, mathematically equivalent formulation that bypasses both bottlenecks by utilizing the block Schur complement and Sylvester's determinant identity. We prove that the computational complexity of both operations collapses from [MATH] to [MATH] per step. We generalize this reduction to Sparse Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Elastic Net, and Group Lasso. Finally, we provide a rigorous numerical stability analysis and evaluate the sampler's efficiency using the Effective Sample Size (ESS) per second. Our empirical benchmarks on high-dimensional datasets confirm a constant speedup exceeding [MATH] while maintaining double-precision numerical equivalence, rendering exact non-smooth NML estimation highly tractable for large-scale statistical inference.
tldr: This paper presents exact Schur-Sylvester dimensionality reductions to accelerate the computation of Normalized Maximum Likelihood codelength for non-smooth estimators like Lasso, using a Propose-and-Project Metropolis-Hastings sampler.
motivation: Exact NML computation for non-smooth estimators is computationally prohibitive due to cubic scaling of projection and volume integration steps.
method: The authors reformulate the projection operator and volume factor using block Schur complement and Sylvester's determinant identity, reducing complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2) per step.
result: The method achieves a constant speedup exceeding 10x while maintaining double-precision numerical equivalence, demonstrated on high-dimensional datasets.
conclusion: The proposed reductions make exact non-smooth NML estimation tractable for large-scale statistical inference.

title: The Serialized Bridge: Understanding And Recovering Llm Serving Performance Under Blackwell Gpu Confidential Computing
authors: Kevin Wang Hang Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.23969v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GPU Confidential Computing (GPU-CC) now preserves GPU-local performance: on NVIDIA B300, BF16 matmul runs at 0.998x of non-confidential performance. Yet LLM serving under Intel TDX plus GPU-CC still loses 13-27% of throughput, and KV-cache restore latency can more than double. This paper studies that gap on two Blackwell platforms, RTX Pro 6000 and B300 HGX, and identifies its dominant cause: the confidential VM-GPU bridge, not GPU compute. We find that GPU-CC turns host/device movement into a serialized, high-setup-cost channel. Secure copies do not gain CUDA-stream concurrency within a context, asynchronous transfers block at the runtime boundary, and small crossings pay a fixed toll. This violates the assumptions of modern inference runtimes, where DMA is expected to be cheap, concurrent, and asynchronous. In vLLM dense decode, the gap closes around 44x-slower small alloc-and-copy operations; targeted patches reject alternative explanations. A scheduling flag recovers 57% of the gap, while a worker-thread drain recovers up to 92% in qualified high-concurrency runs. The same bridge model explains a +131% KV-restore penalty and a 34x model-load slowdown. Blackwell also changes the confidential tenancy unit. We qualify confidential multi-GPU NVSwitch tenants on B300, including 510 GB/s NVLink P2P inside a CVM and concurrent isolated tenants, and identify the remaining fabric-attestation gap for production confidential AI platforms.
tldr: This paper analyzes performance degradation in LLM serving under GPU confidential computing on Blackwell platforms, identifying the serialized VM-GPU bridge as the main bottleneck.
motivation: GPU confidential computing preserves local GPU performance, but LLM serving still suffers significant throughput loss; the paper aims to identify and recover this gap.
method: The authors profile two Blackwell platforms (RTX Pro 6000 and B300 HGX), measure performance under Intel TDX plus GPU-CC, and isolate the cause via targeted patches and scheduling changes.
result: The confidential VM-GPU bridge serializes host/device movement, causing 13-27% throughput loss and up to 2x KV-cache restore latency; a scheduling flag recovers 57% of the gap, and a worker-thread drain recovers up to 92%.
conclusion: The main performance bottleneck is the serialized bridge, not GPU compute; the findings suggest improvements for confidential AI platforms.

The equation of state (EOS) of hydrogen isotopes under extreme conditions is fundamental to planetary science and inertial confinement fusion (ICF), yet experimental constraints across broad thermodynamic regimes remain sparse. We report laser-driven shock measurements on hydrogen and deuterium stat…

tldr: This paper reports experimental measurements of the equation of state of hydrogen and deuterium under extreme conditions using laser-driven shock compression.
motivation: Understanding the equation of state of hydrogen isotopes is crucial for planetary science and inertial confinement fusion, but experimental data across a broad thermodynamic range are sparse.
method: The authors used laser-driven shock waves to compress hydrogen and deuterium samples, combining static pre-compression with dynamic shock loading to access an expanded phase space.
result: They obtained equation of state data for hydrogen and deuterium over a wide range of pressures and temperatures, providing new constraints for theoretical models.
conclusion: The results improve the understanding of hydrogen behavior under extreme conditions relevant to planetary interiors and fusion experiments.

title: Maxwell-Vlasov-Uehling-Uhlenbeck Simulation For Coupled Laser-electron Dynamics In A Metal Irradiated By Ultrashort Intense Laser Pulses
authors: Mizuki Tani, Tomohito Otobe, Yasushi Shinohara, And Kenichi L. Ishikawa
abstract:
Author(s): Mizuki Tani, Tomohito Otobe, Yasushi Shinohara, and Kenichi L. Ishikawa

The description of electron-electron scattering presents challenges in the microscopic modeling of the interaction of ultrashort intense laser pulses with solids. We extend the semiclassical approach based on the Vlasov equation [M. Tani et al.,
tldr: This paper extends a semiclassical Vlasov-based model to include electron-electron scattering via the Uehling-Uhlenbeck collision term for simulating laser-electron dynamics in metals under ultrashort intense laser pulses.
motivation: Accurate modeling of electron-electron scattering is challenging but crucial for understanding the interaction of ultrashort intense laser pulses with solids.
method: The authors extend their previous Vlasov equation approach by incorporating the Uehling-Uhlenbeck collision term to account for dynamic electron-electron scattering, and solve the resulting Maxwell-Vlasov-Uehling-Uhlenbeck system.
result: The simulation captures coupled laser-electron dynamics including electron-electron scattering effects, providing insights into the microscopic response of metals to intense laser pulses.
conclusion: The extended model improves the description of electron dynamics in laser-irradiated metals, but the work is focused on computational plasma physics and laser-matter interaction, not on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

motivation: To understand the thermoelectric transport properties of shape-memory Heusler alloys, which have potential for multifunctional applications.

result: Observed a large anomalous Nernst effect and its dependence on temperature and magnetic field, correlated with the structural phase transition.
conclusion: The anomalous Nernst effect is sensitive to the martensitic transformation and can be used to probe electronic structure changes in shape-memory alloys.

motivation: To realize acoustic complementary media experimentally, which has been challenging due to the need for simultaneous engineering of mass density and bulk modulus.

tldr: This paper studies pressure-induced structural changes and superconductivity in the one-dimensional van der Waals material InSeI.
motivation: To explore the pressure-tunable optical and electronic properties of chalcohalides, specifically the piezochromism and potential superconductivity in InSeI.
method: High-pressure experiments using diamond anvil cells combined with in situ optical spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and electrical transport measurements.
result: Observation of pressure-induced amorphization and polyamorphic transitions, with superconductivity emerging at high pressures.
conclusion: The study reveals a rich pressure-temperature phase diagram and demonstrates that InSeI is a platform for studying structure-property relationships in low-dimensional materials.

title: Coupled Maxwell Equations And Semiclassical Electronic And Molecular Dynamics Simulation For Analyzing Laser Ablation Of Silicon Thin Films

motivation: To enable practical simulation of laser-material interactions at the atomic scale, capturing both electromagnetic wave propagation and electronic/ionic dynamics.
method: A coupled simulation scheme integrating Maxwell equations with semiclassical electronic and molecular dynamics based on the electron force field model.
result: The method allows description of interaction dynamics among electrons, ions, and electromagnetic waves during laser ablation.
conclusion: The coupled simulation provides a practical tool for analyzing laser ablation of silicon thin films.

title: Predicting Instantaneous Friction From Friction Damping Coefficients In Underdamped Sliding
authors: Chengdong Sun, Yi Tao, Zaoqi Duan, Kai Chen, Quan Han, Yajing Kan, Zhonghua Ni, Zhiyong Wei, Yan Zhang, And Yunfei Chen

Friction accounts for nearly one-third of global energy consumption. While the coefficient of friction is widely used to quantify energy dissipation in sliding contacts, its strong dependence on sliding velocity limits its effectiveness in predicting instantaneous friction forces and friction-induce…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065508] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies friction dynamics in underdamped sliding systems, focusing on predicting instantaneous friction from damping coefficients.
motivation: Friction accounts for nearly one-third of global energy consumption, and the coefficient of friction's dependence on sliding velocity limits its predictive power for instantaneous friction forces.
method: The authors develop a model that uses friction damping coefficients to predict instantaneous friction in underdamped sliding contacts.
result: The model provides a method to estimate instantaneous friction forces more accurately than traditional coefficient-based approaches.
conclusion: The proposed approach improves prediction of friction-induced energy dissipation, which could aid in designing more efficient mechanical systems.

title: Unsteady Phase Waves In The One-dimensional Swarmalator Model With Inertia
authors: Kevin O'keeffe
abstract:
Author(s): Kevin O'Keeffe

We study a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia. Previous studies have focused almost exclusively on the overdamped limit. We find inertia introduces an unsteady collective state in which the rainbow order parameters undergo multiharmonic oscillations. This “thrashing” phase wave bifurcate…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064210] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia, discovering a new unsteady collective state called 'thrashing' phase waves.
motivation: Previous studies of swarmalators focused on the overdamped limit; this work introduces inertia to explore new collective dynamics.
method: The authors analyze a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia using analytical and numerical methods, examining the bifurcation of rainbow order parameters.
result: Inertia leads to multiharmonic oscillations in the rainbow order parameters, giving rise to a 'thrashing' phase wave state.
conclusion: Inertia fundamentally alters the collective behavior of swarmalators, producing unsteady dynamics not seen in the overdamped regime.

title: Fractional Degree Centrality For Directed Networks
authors: Kang-Ju Lee, Ki-Ahm Lee, Woong Kook, And Taehun Lee

Degree centrality is one of the most fundamental measures of local importance in directed networks. When [MATH], the fractional centrality reduces to the out-degree centrality. …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064310] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a fractional version of degree centrality for directed networks using the fractional directed Laplacian.
motivation: Degree centrality is a fundamental measure in network analysis, but its fractional generalization may capture non-local influences in directed networks.
method: The authors define fractional degree centrality via the fractional directed Laplacian with a parameter α, and analyze its properties.
result: The fractional centrality reduces to out-degree centrality when α=1, and exhibits non-local behavior for other α values.

title: Emergence Of A Fluctuation-driven Cooperative Solidlike Phase In Potts Model Monolayers
authors: Alexander J. Devanny And Laura J. Kaufman

Cellular Potts model (CPM) simulations display significant variation in dynamics, structural ordering, and observed phase transitions. [Phys. Rev. E 113, 064410] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies phase transitions in cellular Potts model monolayers, focusing on a fluctuation-driven cooperative solidlike phase.
motivation: To understand the variability in dynamics and phase transitions observed in cellular Potts model simulations due to differences in implementation.
method: The authors perform cellular Potts model simulations with varying definitions of cell perimeter and area constraints, analyzing structural ordering and dynamics.
result: They identify a fluctuation-driven cooperative solidlike phase that emerges under certain conditions, distinct from conventional solid phases.
conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of implementation details in CPM simulations and reveal a new type of phase behavior in monolayer systems.

result: Insights into melting and supercooling mechanisms at atomic scale.
conclusion: The study clarifies microscopic phase transition mechanisms, aiding design of thermal storage materials.

authors: João N. C. Especial And Patrícia F. N. Faísca

Knotted proteins embed a physical (i.e., open) knot within their native structures. For decades, significant effort has been devoted to elucidating the functional role of knots in proteins, yet no consensus has been reached. Here, using extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple struc…

tldr: This paper studies how topological knots in proteins enhance kinetic stability using Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: To understand the functional role of knots in proteins, which remains debated despite decades of study.
method: Extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple structure-based model for knotted proteins.
result: Topological knots increase the kinetic stability of proteins by raising the free energy barrier to unfolding.
conclusion: Knots may serve a biological role by enhancing protein robustness against mechanical or thermal denaturation.

title: Characterizing Emergent Multiscale Dynamics In Colloidal Nanoparticle Gels
authors: William D. Brackett, Zachary M. Sherman, Felix Lehmkühler, Thomas M. Truskett, And Delia J. Milliron
abstract:
Author(s): William D. Brackett, Zachary M. Sherman, Felix Lehmkühler, Thomas M. Truskett, and Delia J. Milliron

Characterizing the dynamics of nanoparticle gel networks demands a spatiotemporal resolution that no single technique can provide. This Perspective describes the opportunities to address this challenge using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy at fourth-generation light sources combined with complementary experimental and simulation tools. This should move the field beyond descriptive fundamental studies toward mechanistic understanding and design of nanoparticle gels with adaptive and programmable behaviors.


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 061001] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This perspective discusses using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy at fourth-generation light sources to study multiscale dynamics in colloidal nanoparticle gels.
motivation: Understanding the dynamics of nanoparticle gel networks requires spatiotemporal resolution beyond any single technique, motivating a combined experimental and simulation approach.
method: The paper proposes using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy at advanced light sources, complemented by other experimental methods and simulations.
result: No new results are presented; it is a perspective outlining opportunities for future research.
conclusion: The field can move from descriptive studies to mechanistic understanding and design of adaptive nanoparticle gels.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews geospace science advances made using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: To summarize the scientific contributions of the Arecibo Observatory in upper atmospheric and ionospheric research over its 50-year operation.
method: The paper reviews incoherent scatter radar theory and presents key results from Arecibo's radar, lidar, and optical instruments in studies of plasma physics, space weather, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
result: The review highlights advances in understanding ionospheric dynamics, metal layers, and coupling processes, enabled by Arecibo's unique capabilities.
conclusion: Arecibo's legacy includes foundational contributions to geospace science, but the paper does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: A colloquium on multimessenger astronomy with continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and future detectors.
motivation: To discuss detection prospects for continuous gravitational waves and their implications for astrophysics and condensed matter physics.
method: Review of current and future gravitational-wave detectors and simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: Highlights the potential for multimessenger observations to probe dense environments of neutron stars.
conclusion: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier for multimessenger astronomy, with strong connections to other fields.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties provide crucial tests of nuclear physics under extreme conditions.
method: The paper reviews recent observational constraints from gravitational-wave signals (binary neutron star mergers) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to theoretical predictions of the nuclear equation of state.
result: The review summarizes current constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, and discusses how they inform the equation of state at and beyond nuclear densities.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of dense matter, but the paper does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

abstract:

method: Narrative and reflective essay based on the author's experiences.
result: No new technical results; a retrospective on the development of Hopfield networks and their impact.
conclusion: Physics is a way of thinking that can inspire interdisciplinary discoveries.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
